- Budget event: `PERF-001-P8-B1`, authorized by entry to P8 (phase file, Performance candidate `PERF-001` recheck).
- Workload: unchanged (Node control, `buildos version`, `buildos help`, `buildos version --json`). The workload does not have to change to include ported commands: the question is the cost of loading the bundle, which now holds every ported domain and the PDF reader, and these commands pay that cost in full. So no profile version increment.

The release build (`scripts/release-build.ts`) differs only by the version and revision define (a trial release-define bundle is 3,309,964 bytes against 3,310,039); it was not used, because the profile names the default build. The P1 result expired at this recheck by its own expiry rule.

### Pass 1 Result (t21)

- Result ID: `PERF-001-P8-R1`.
- Exact profile binding: `PERF-001` v1.1, `sha256:67de4a287df0a5f6d7cd648181c8751ff2a26ecb73aa3b3bde09363b79c00761`.
- Build and evidence fingerprint: as in the packet. The instrument reported the same bundle and instrument digests.

| Workload | n | Excluded | Min | p25 | Median | p75 | p90 | Max | IQR | Median 95% interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Node control | 50 | 0 | 27.00 | 27.72 | 28.46 | 28.94 | 29.68 | 31.68 | 1.23 | 28.03 to 28.81 |
| `buildos version` | 50 | 0 | 65.28 | 67.57 | 68.24 | 69.87 | 71.48 | 74.09 | 2.31 | 67.85 to 68.64 |
| `buildos help` | 50 | 0 | 66.38 | 68.05 | 68.72 | 70.38 | 72.29 | 77.80 | 2.34 | 68.30 to 69.50 |
| `buildos version --json` | 50 | 0 | 66.95 | 67.70 | 68.41 | 69.60 | 72.52 | 74.07 | 1.90 | 67.82 to 69.13 |

All times are milliseconds of wall-clock time, from spawn to exit.

- Observed distribution: BuildOS overhead over the Node control, as a difference of medians, is 39.78 ms for `version`, 40.26 ms for `help`, and 39.95 ms for `version --json`: about 58% of each run. Node startup itself is about 28.5 ms. As context only (not comparable): P1 measured 1.25 to 1.66 ms of overhead with a 12,810-byte bundle.
- Uncertainty and exclusions: each BuildOS median interval lies wholly above the control interval, so the overhead is distinguishable from noise. The overhead is a difference of two medians, and no interval of that difference was computed. The two median intervals bound it loosely: for `version`, the control interval (28.03 to 28.81 ms) and the `version` interval (67.85 to 68.64 ms) leave an overhead between 39.0 and 40.6 ms (review round 2 wording: an earlier text said "uncertain to about 1 ms", which no computed interval supports). No run was excluded and no trimming was applied.
- Where the time goes (static facts, not a measurement): the PDF reader (`unpdf` with pdf.js) is 2,410,510 of the bundle's 3,310,039 bytes (73%). `src/adapters/intake-parsers.ts` imports `unpdf` statically, so every command loads and compiles it, also `version`. One CPU profile of `buildos version` (`node --cpu-prof`) put most of its time in Node's own module loading and compiling, which the profile cannot attribute to a package; it was not used as a result.
- Budget ledger: above.
- Outcome: `pass`
- Outcome reason: the distribution and uncertainty exist for every workload, with no exclusion, and every non-sacrificable constraint held: every counted run exited 0 with the expected output; the full test suite passed on the same source (see [Check Results (P8 Stage 2)](#check-results-p8-stage-2)), and that run rebuilt a bundle with the same SHA-256; the dependency guard passed; the commands make no network call; the raw record holds timings and machine class only.
- Findings: none against a target (there is none). Observation for the owner: the bundle-load cost is now the larger part of a short command. (Review round 2: an earlier text compared this with the P1 overhead as "about 24-fold"; the two runs have different fingerprints, a 12,810-byte bundle then, so they are not comparable, and the comparison is withdrawn.)
- Owner or reviewer disposition: agent review below; owner decision through owner question 1.
- Supported-scope limit: the three commands from the bundle, Node 24.22.3, this one Apple M2 Pro macOS arm64 machine, warm file cache. It says nothing about Linux, Windows, x64, a cold cache, the `npx` path, or a long-running domain command.
- Expiry: at any material change trigger in the profile, or at the next release that changes the bundle.
- Later result: none yet.

### Decision

Characterization only. No target is set, and this pass by itself does not require a change before `0.1.0`. The P1 decision named the change to consider if the overhead became a large share of the run: lazy loading inside the one bundle. The overhead is now about 58% of a short command, so that question goes to the owner (owner question 1). Context for it: about 40 ms per command is small next to an agent tool call and next to the `npx` resolution that every wrapper call goes through, which PERF-001 does not measure and `PERF-002` measures only for the first run. A lazy load of the PDF reader would be the obvious candidate, because it is 73% of the bundle and only `intake convert` of a PDF needs it; its saving is not measured, because this task changes no code and the profile spends no correction attempt on a product change.

### Agent Review

- Deterministic method: `make-docs run performance evidence validate --target-root .` (see [Check Results (P8 Stage 2)](#check-results-p8-stage-2)).
- `PERF-RULE-015`: `characterize-now` still fits: the release candidate exists and a decision on bundling is due before `0.1.0`.
- `PERF-RULE-016`: the environment supports only the within-pass comparison with the Node control on this machine. The P1 figures are context, not a comparison.
- `PERF-RULE-017`: impact moderate at most (tens of milliseconds per call), no finding against a target, no waiver. Supported scope as stated.
- Limits: the review is by the implementing agent, not an independent reviewer. It certifies no other proof mode.

### Owner Questions (P8 Stage 2)

1. Startup cost before `0.1.0`. A short command now takes about 68 ms on the measured machine, about 40 ms of it loading the 3.3 MB bundle; the PDF reader is 73% of the bundle and loads on every command. Options: (A) ship `0.1.0` as it is and plan a lazy load of the PDF reader (dynamic `import()` inside the one bundle) for a later release, with a new `PERF-001` recheck then; (B) make that change before `0.1.0`, which needs a code change, a new golden and reproducibility run, and another `PERF-001` budget event. Recommendation: A, because 40 ms is small next to an agent tool call and the `npx` resolution of each wrapper call, and a bundling change now would reopen the release evidence. `PERF-002` (first run through `npx`) may still change this answer.
2. A global `buildos` overrides the project pin (F-P8-S2-01). Options: (A) keep the wrapper order (`PATH` first, which makes offline installs work) and document it, as this pass does; (B) change the wrappers to prefer the pinned version and run a `PATH` `buildos` only when its version equals the pin. Recommendation: A for `0.1.0`, because B is a wrapper change after the P6 reviews and the offline path relies on A; record B for W2 update.

### Release Job Graph After Round 1

| Job | Permissions and secrets | Code it runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `resolve` | `contents: read` | Its own shell script and `git` only; outputs the one SHA, the tag, the mode, and the default-branch SHA |
| `verify` | `contents: read`; no secret | The candidate's build, tests, and gates (`release-gate.ts`), deny-list with an invented list; uploads only on success |
| `deny-list` (release) | `contents: read`; real list from environment `buildos-deny-list` | The default branch's `check-deny-list.mjs` and `release-stage-check.ts digest`, Node built-ins only; candidate tree and tarball as data |
| `stage` (release) | `contents: read`, `id-token: write`; environment `buildos-npm-stage` | `release-stage-check.ts stage` (Node built-ins) from a sparse checkout of the SHA, then `npm stage publish` from an empty folder |
| `sbom` (release) | `contents: write` | `gh release upload` |
| `discard` (release, on a deny-list failure) | `actions: write` | `gh api -X DELETE` of the run's artifact |

### Deny-List Secret Design

Choice: the real list lives in a GitHub environment whose deployment refs are the default branch and the `v*` tags, and the jobs that receive it run only trusted code (option b, with the trusted-code rule of option a). Why: GitHub states that "any user with write access to your repository has read access to all secrets configured in your repository" (docs.github.com, Secure use reference), because a writer can change the workflow file on their own branch. Running the scanner from the default branch (option a alone) cannot stop that: the edited workflow on the branch decides what runs. An environment's deployment-ref rule is checked by GitHub before the job gets a runner, and the job reads the environment's secrets only after that ("Any protection rules configured for the environment must pass before a job referencing the environment is sent to a runner", docs.github.com, Deployment environments). So only the protected default branch and release tags can reach the list. Inside those jobs, nothing from the candidate runs: no `npm` (so no `.npmrc` or `package.json` scripts are read by npm), no build, only the scanner with Node built-ins, which reads the tree and the tarball as data. In the release run the scanner comes from the default branch at the SHA that `resolve` found, and it first checks that the tarball is the reviewed one, so the list is checked against exactly the bytes that are staged. Fail closed stays: a missing or empty list fails both real-list jobs. Every other push and pull request, from a fork too, runs the scanner with an invented list (home-folder paths, unread files, the self-test) and shows a notice that the real list runs after merge; dry-run branches plant the deny-list failure with an invented list. Cost: a client name on a feature branch is found when it reaches the default branch or a release, not on the branch; a maintainer can run the check before pushing with `--list-file`. The environment and its rules are owner actions (below); until they exist, the default-branch job runs in an environment that GitHub creates with no rules and fails closed without the secret.

### Owner Actions

Settings paths from docs.github.com, read on 2026-11-24. No agent changes these settings. They are also in `SECURITY.md` (Owner Settings for Releases).

- History rewrite and visibility (owner decision A): review the orchestrator's rewritten copy, force-push it, then make the repository public (Settings > General > Danger Zone > Change repository visibility). Then do the SHA mapping task above.
- Default branch: Settings > Rules > Rulesets > New ruleset > New branch ruleset; target the default branch; "Block force pushes" and "Require status checks to pass" (the three-OS test jobs and "Client-name deny list"). Do this after the force-push of the rewrite.
- Release tags: Settings > Rules > Rulesets > New ruleset > New tag ruleset; target `v*`; "Restrict creations", "Restrict updates", "Restrict deletions"; only the maintainer on the bypass list. GitHub has no separate release permission: write access can manage releases, so the tag rules decide who can make a release tag.
- Immutable releases: Settings, section Releases > "Enable release immutability" (generally available since 2025-10-28).
- Environments: Settings > Environments > New environment `buildos-deny-list`; Deployment branches and tags > "Selected branches and tags" > the default branch and tag rule `v*`; add the secret `BUILDOS_DENY_LIST` there. New environment `buildos-npm-stage` with tag rule `v*` only. Then delete the repository secret `BUILDOS_DENY_LIST` (Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions).
- Private vulnerability reporting, after the repository is public: Settings > Security and quality > Advanced Security > "Private vulnerability reporting" > Enable.
- npm: the First Publication steps in `toolkits/buildos/AGENTS.md` (placeholder, trusted publisher, publishing access, `latest` check, deprecation).

### Release Flow After Round 2

1. Maintainer: version, dry run, inspect the tarball, commit the `reviewed` entry (ledger).
2. Maintainer: tag `v<version>` and a draft GitHub Release.
3. `prepare` (dispatch from the default branch): `resolve` (no repository code) → `verify` (candidate code, no secret, `contents: read`) → `deny-list` (trusted code, real list, `actions: read`) → `attach` (trusted code, `contents: write`): tarball and SBOM on the draft.
4. Maintainer: review the draft, publish it (immutable).
5. `release` (published event): `resolve` → `verify` (rebuild must equal the reviewed digest) → `deny-list` → `stage` (trusted code, `id-token: write` and `actions: read`, environment `buildos-npm-stage` with a required reviewer who approves the job first): download the release asset, check it, `npm stage publish` with a clean npm configuration.
6. Maintainer: approve the npm stage with 2FA after the recorded publication approval. `discard` deletes this run's artifact after a deny-list failure.

### Owner Actions (Round 2)

In this order; exact paths in `toolkits/buildos/SECURITY.md` (Owner Settings for Releases), verified against docs.github.com on 2026-11-24.

1. Finish the history rewrite and make the repository public (Settings > General > Danger Zone > Change repository visibility). On GitHub Free, environments work only in a public repository.
2. Create the environment `buildos-deny-list` with deployment refs branch `main` and tag `v*` (Settings > Environments > New environment).
3. Add its environment secret `BUILDOS_DENY_LIST_ENV`: `gh secret set BUILDOS_DENY_LIST_ENV --env buildos-deny-list --repo brucewaynedecoy/build-os < <list file outside the repository>` (the value comes from stdin and is not echoed).
4. Delete the repository secret: `gh secret delete BUILDOS_DENY_LIST --repo brucewaynedecoy/build-os`.
5. Create the environment `buildos-npm-stage`: required reviewer the maintainer, Prevent self-review off (one maintainer), Allow administrators to bypass off, deployment ref tag `v*`.
6. Default branch ruleset: restrict deletions, block force pushes, required pull request (1 approval, code-owner review), required checks `test (ubuntu-latest, Node 24)`, `test (macos-latest, Node 24)`, `test (windows-latest, Node 24)`, `OSV scan of package-lock.json`, `Make Docs contract (pinned range bounds)`, `Deny list (invented list, every push and pull request)`; with one maintainer, a bypass "For pull requests only".
7. Tag ruleset on `v*`: restrict creations, updates, deletions; bypass the maintainer only.
8. Settings > General > Releases > Enable release immutability.
9. Private vulnerability reporting (Settings > Advanced Security), after the repository is public.
10. npm First Publication (AGENTS.md), then the release procedure.

### What the In-Job Checks Can and Cannot Verify

With the job token (`GITHUB_TOKEN`, an installation token of the GitHub Actions app):

| Item | Checked in the job | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Effective active rules of `main` (deletion, force push, pull request with 1 approval and code-owner review, the six required checks) | Yes, fail closed | `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rules/branches/main`, Metadata read |
| An active tag ruleset for `refs/tags/v*` with no exclusion that restricts creation, update, and deletion | Yes, fail closed | `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets?targets=tag` and each ruleset by ID, Metadata read |
| Environment deployment refs, required reviewer, approval of this run | Yes, fail closed (since round 2) | Environment, deployment-branch-policy, and run-approval endpoints, Actions read |
| The published release is immutable, holds exactly the tarball and the SBOM, with GitHub's digests | Yes, fail closed | Releases endpoints, Contents read |
| Who may bypass a ruleset | No | `bypass_actors` is returned only to a user with write access to the ruleset |
| The repository's release-immutability setting | No | `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/immutable-releases` needs Administration read, which a workflow cannot grant; the release's own `immutable` flag is checked instead |
| Who holds write access; whether Prevent self-review is on | No | Owner settings; the npm two-factor approval is the last check |

### Final Ordered Owner Checklist

From `toolkits/buildos/SECURITY.md` (Owner Settings for Releases) and `toolkits/buildos/AGENTS.md` (First Publication). No agent does any of these.

1. Delete the repository secret `BUILDOS_DENY_LIST` (`gh secret delete BUILDOS_DENY_LIST --repo brucewaynedecoy/build-os`), and check `gh secret list`.
2. Finish the history rewrite (owner decision A) and force-push it; then add the SHA mapping note.
3. Make the repository public.
4. Create the branch ruleset `main` (deletions, force pushes, pull request with 1 approval and code-owner review, the six checks; bypass: Repository admin, For pull requests only).
5. Create the tag ruleset `release tags` for `v*` (creation, update, deletion; bypass: Repository admin, Always allow).
6. Turn on release immutability.
7. Verify steps 1 to 6 (Rulesets page, the three `gh api` reads).
8. Create the environment `buildos-deny-list` (deployment refs: branch `main`, tag `v*`).
9. Create the environment `buildos-npm-stage` (required reviewer the maintainer, Prevent self-review off, administrators cannot bypass, deployment ref tag `v*`).
10. Add the environment secret `BUILDOS_DENY_LIST_ENV` to `buildos-deny-list`.
11. Turn on private vulnerability reporting.
12. npm First Publication: stage and approve the placeholder `0.0.0-reserved.0`, configure the trusted publisher (staging only, environment `buildos-npm-stage`), set "Require two-factor authentication and disallow tokens".
13. Release `0.1.0`: dry run on the reference runner, inspect the tarball, commit the `reviewed` entry, tag `v0.1.0` and a draft release, the prepare run, review and publish the draft, approve the staging job, then approve the npm stage with 2FA after the recorded publication approval; check the dist-tags and deprecate the placeholders.

### First Exercised Only by a Real Prepare or Release Run

- The real-list scan with the environment secret, in the release `deny-list` job and in the `buildos-deny-list.yml` real-list job on `main`.
- The ruleset check and the environment check against the real repository settings and the real job token (only the fake API ran here).
- `find-draft` and `attach` against a real draft (uploads by release ID, GitHub's computed digests on the uploaded assets).
- The required reviewer's approval of `buildos-npm-stage` and the run-approval check.
- `download-asset` against a published immutable release: which of the two response forms GitHub uses, and that GitHub lists a digest for both assets.
- The SBOM byte comparison between the prepare run's attached SBOM and the release run's verify SBOM on the reference runner.
- The npm OIDC token, `npm stage publish --provenance`, the provenance statement, the stage ID, and the dist-tag of the first publish.
- `discard` after a real-list failure.

That line holds `"<npx.cmd folder>\\node.exe" "<npx-cli.js>" <arguments>`, and npm's `npx.cmd` takes the `npx-cli.js` path from `npm prefix -g` (for example `%APPDATA%\npm\node_modules\npm\bin\npx-cli.js` after `npm install -g npm`), which the helper cannot know without starting a program. Exact failure case: with `npx.cmd` at `C:\Program Files\nodejs\npx.cmd` and no global npm, the arguments `-y`, `@brucewaynedecoy/buildos@1.2.3`, and one argument of 7,600 `x` give a real `npx.cmd` line of about 7,740 characters (`"C:\Program Files\nodejs\\node.exe" "C:\Program Files\nodejs\\node_modules\npm\bin\npx-cli.js" ` and the arguments escaped once) and a `cmd.exe` line of about 7,690 characters, both under 8,191, but the estimate is 8,308 characters and the check refuses it (exit 2); `test/wrappers.test.ts` "finding 11: knows when Command Prompt cannot take the npx line" expects that refusal. A fix reads npm's global prefix from its config files without starting npm, or measures the line in a different way ([Pin-First Wrappers Final Check](#pin-first-wrappers-final-check), finding 6).

### Pin-First Wrappers

Replaced by [Pin-First Wrappers Review Round 1](#pin-first-wrappers-review-round-1): the version check below started the program on `PATH`, and it is gone. This section is kept as the record of `f6adf5f`.

- How the wrapper learns the version: it runs `buildos version --json` on the first `buildos` on `PATH` that is not a project wrapper, with no input and its stderr not shown. It uses that program only when the command exits `0` within 20 seconds and the JSON envelope reports `ok` true, command `version`, and exactly the pinned version. Another version, a failure, no output, output that is not the envelope, more than 64 KiB of output, or no answer in time: the wrapper runs the pinned version through `npx`. The `version --json` envelope is the stable automation contract and the same in the Go tools, so the check reads no free text.
- Cost: one extra start of the program on `PATH`, and only when one is there. With no program on `PATH`, nothing changes.
- A `dev` pin (a source build) has no published version: it runs only a program that reports `dev`, else the dev message and exit `3`.
- Safety rules kept: the PATH search skips the wrapper itself and every project wrapper; an empty or unsafe pin is refused; the Node.js version message is the same; `!` handling in the `.cmd` forms; exact exit code pass-through. The loop guard stays set during the check, so a program that only calls a project wrapper again fails the check.
- On macOS and Linux, a `buildos` on `PATH` now needs Node.js 24 or newer for the wrapper to read the pin. An npm-installed `buildos` needs it anyway.
- Code: `system/.os/scripts/buildos`, `buildos.cmd`, `pinned-version.cjs`, and the three legacy scripts with their `.cmd` forms. `buildos init` installs them from the `system/` package content (`WRAPPER_FILES` in `toolkits/buildos/src/core/init/content.ts`); the file list and the package file list did not change.
- Tests: `toolkits/buildos/test/wrappers.test.ts` (a PATH program with the pinned version runs; another version does not run and `npx` runs; six failed version checks; dev pin both ways; the legacy notice once, first on stderr, with arguments, stdout, and exit code unchanged; Windows-only cases for a folder name with `!` and a legacy `.cmd` script), and `toolkits/buildos/test/init-review-4.test.ts` (P6-R4-09 now pins a version first).

## Pin-First Wrappers Review Round 1

Review of `f6adf5f` (the pin-first wrappers). The orchestrator accepted every finding and decided the design change on 2026-11-25: the wrapper no longer starts the program on `PATH` to learn its version. All checks below ran on 2026-11-25 on one Apple M2 Pro macOS arm64 machine with Node 26.13.1 and npm 11.20.0. Windows CI did not run on this round. Nothing was pushed, published, staged, tagged, or released, and no repository or npm setting changed.

### Wrapper Design (Final)

- The wrapper never starts a program to learn its version. `pinned-version.cjs` reads `package.json` files only.
- Order, after the Node.js check and the manifest contract: (1) a local npm install, `node_modules/@brucewaynedecoy/buildos` in the project folder (the parent of `.os/`), then in npm's local project folder (the first folder up from the current folder with a `package.json` file or a `node_modules` folder, as npm's own config finds it); (2) the first `buildos` on `PATH` that is not this wrapper and not a project wrapper, when it is an npm install; (3) `npx -y @brucewaynedecoy/buildos@<pin>` with `npm_config_bin_links=true`.
- macOS and Linux: the `sh` wrapper finds the `PATH` candidate (POSIX `PATH` rules; a relative entry gets a leading `./`). The helper follows all links of the candidate (`realpath`), walks up to the nearest `package.json`, and accepts it only when the package's `buildos` bin file has that same real path.
- Windows: the helper searches `PATH` (quotes and `;` handled as Windows does). It accepts a `.cmd` shim only when `node_modules\@brucewaynedecoy\buildos` is next to it (a global install), or, for a shim in `node_modules\.bin`, when the package is in that `node_modules` folder. The shim never runs.
- A package counts only when its `package.json` is a regular file (no link), at most 256 KiB, valid UTF-8 with no byte order mark, strict JSON, with the name `@brucewaynedecoy/buildos` and exactly the pinned version, and its `buildos` bin file (a string or object `bin`) is a relative path to a regular file inside the package after all links are followed.
- Dispatch: `node <bin file> <arguments>` with the same Node.js that ran the helper (`process.execPath`), in the caller's working folder. The `sh` wrapper gets three lines (`run`, the Node.js path, the bin file) and `exec`s them only when both paths are absolute; a path with a control character is never accepted. On Windows the helper starts Node.js directly, with no `cmd.exe` in between. Verification and dispatch use the same package folder, so there is no second `PATH` lookup, no probe process, no timeout, and no output limit.
- `dev` pin: the same no-execute rule. It accepts an install of a source build, whose `package.json` version is `0.0.0-dev` (the version in `toolkits/buildos/package.json`; for example `npm link` from the source folder, or `npm install <source folder>` in the project). Else exit `3` with a message that names the two ways that work. This is simpler than a `dev`-only probe with a process-tree kill and an output limit, and it runs no code from `PATH`.
- Kept: the `PATH` search skips the wrapper itself (file identity) and every project wrapper; the loop guard; an empty or unsafe pin is refused; the Node.js message; exact arguments and exit code; `!`, `%`, space, and quote handling in `.cmd`; no bashisms (checked with `dash`).
- Residual risk, stated in `SECURITY.md` (Project wrappers): a copy of the pinned version that npm finds and the wrapper does not accept (a nested copy, a workspace root, a `prefix` setting, a `package.json` that the strict read refuses, a global `bin/buildos` that is not the package's bin file, an npx cache made with bin links off). Then npm can start another `buildos` from `PATH`.

## Pin-First Wrappers Review Round 2

Review of `9913d62` (the pin-first wrappers after round 1). CI on `9913d62`: Windows passed; ubuntu failed ([run 45720263841](https://github.com/brucewaynedecoy/build-os/actions/runs/45720263841), finding 1). The orchestrator accepted every finding and decided on 2026-11-25 that the program that runs checks itself, instead of a perfect file inspection by the wrapper. All checks below ran on 2026-11-25 on one Apple silicon Mac (macOS, Node.js 26.13.1, npm 11.20.0). CI run links in this file from before the repository cutover name runs of the earlier repository; after the cutover, those runs are in the private archive repository `brucewaynedecoy/build-os-archive`.

### Self-Check Design

- Variable: `BUILDOS_REQUIRE_VERSION`. Every project wrapper sets it on every start (a local install, a `buildos` on `PATH`, `npx`) to the pinned version, or `dev` for a `dev` pin. The code base has no other naming rule; the name follows `BUILDOS_WRAPPER_ACTIVE`.
- Check: `src/cli/required-version.ts`, called first in `src/cli/main.ts`. The command modules (`run.ts`, `io.ts`) load only after the check, so no command code, output, or file access comes before it. The legacy-name entry files import the same bundle, so they go through the same check, before their notice line.
- Refusal: when the variable is set, not empty, and not exactly the build identity that `buildos version` reports (a release version or `dev`). Nothing on stdout. Stderr: `BuildOS stopped: this project needs BuildOS <required>, but BuildOS <started> started. Nothing ran.` and `Fix the BuildOS install so that version <required> runs, then run the project wrapper (.os/scripts/buildos) again. Or set buildos_version in .os/manifest.json to the version that you want to use.` Exit code `3` (PRD 20: a required input, the pinned version, cannot be loaded; the wrapper already uses `3` for a pin it cannot use). A required value with characters outside `[0-9A-Za-z.+-]` is shown JSON-quoted.
- JSON form: with `--json` on the command line, stdout has the failure envelope (`ok` false, `command` the first argument after legacy-name mapping, the program's own `version` and `source_revision`, `root` and `mode` empty, `write_status` `not_requested`, `result` null, one diagnostic `version_mismatch` with the message and the fixes as `correction`), and stderr is empty.
- No fallback after a refusal. After the check, the program removes `BUILDOS_REQUIRE_VERSION` from its own environment. An unset or empty variable means no check, so a direct `buildos` run and the golden compare are unchanged.
- Bin links (finding 12): the override stays, because without it a user with `npm_config_bin_links=false` would get a refusal or a loop stop instead of a working run. The wrapper keeps the caller's own settings in `BUILDOS_SAVED_npm_config_bin_links` and `BUILDOS_SAVED_NPM_CONFIG_BIN_LINKS` (on Windows, every case and spelling) and sets `BUILDOS_NPM_BIN_LINKS_OVERRIDE=1`. The program, in the same place where it removes `BUILDOS_REQUIRE_VERSION`, removes the override and puts the caller's values back. Saved values without the override mark are removed and not applied.
- The wrapper's `package.json` read stays as the cheap way to choose a candidate. It is no longer a security boundary. The threat model is stated in `SECURITY.md` (Project wrappers) and PRD 06.

### Findings and Dispositions (Pin-First Round 2)

| Finding | What was done | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (blocker) dash read `-tools/npx` as options | The `sh` wrapper finds `node` and `npx` with `command -v` and starts them by path (a relative result gets a leading `./`), never by bare name. The `PATH` search for `buildos` moved into `pinned-version.cjs` (finding 9), which uses absolute paths. | `test/wrappers.test.ts` "finds an npm install, node, and npx through relative PATH entries that start with -", once with `/bin/sh` and once with `/bin/dash` (the dash case fails on the old wrapper) |

## Package Name `build-os` (2026-11-26)

Owner decision of 2026-11-26: the npm package is published as the unscoped name `build-os` under the npm account `brucewaynedecoy`, not as `@brucewaynedecoy/buildos`. `npm install build-os` and `npm install -g build-os` must work. Checked on 2026-11-26: `build-os`, `buildos`, and `@brucewaynedecoy/buildos` did not exist on npm. Nothing was published under the earlier name, so no published version changes. The register entry is `Q-017` in [PRD 03](../../prd/03-open-questions-and-risk-register.md).

Orchestrator decisions of the same day:

1. The command name stays `buildos`, and the three legacy names stay as they are. No command behavior changes.
2. One more `bin` entry, `build-os`, points to `dist/buildos.js`, the same file as `buildos`. npx runs the `bin` named after the package when a package has several, so `npx -y build-os@<version> <command>` needs it. `dist/buildos.js` never reads the name it was started under (`src/cli/invocation.ts`; only the legacy entry files pass a name), so `build-os` runs as `buildos` on macOS, Linux, and Windows (npm's `.cmd` and `.ps1` shims run `node <path>/dist/buildos.js`): no notice line and no domain added. `build-os` is not a legacy name and does not go away in `0.3.0`.
3. The tarball is `build-os-<version>.tgz`, the name that `npm pack` gives; `scripts/release-ledger.ts` `tarballName` derives it from the package name. The SBOM file stays `buildos-<version>.cdx.json`: no script derives it from the package name. The SBOM component is `build-os` with the purl `pkg:npm/build-os@<version>` (npm's SBOM sets the purl).
4. `--access public` stays in every documented `npm stage publish` command and in the workflow's `stage` job. It is the default for an unscoped package and does no harm.

What changed:

- `toolkits/buildos/package.json` and `package-lock.json`: the name `build-os` (both places in the lockfile); the `bin` `build-os`. `repository` points to `https://github.com/brucewaynedecoy/build-os` (the package has no `homepage` or `bugs` field; none was added).
- Source: the `npx` command that `init` prints (`src/cli/commands/init.ts`, `src/core/init/init.ts`), the `dev` recovery message (`src/cli/required-version.ts`).
- Wrappers (`system/.os/scripts/`): `pinned-version.cjs` accepts only a package whose `package.json` name is `build-os`; the local lookup looks in `node_modules/build-os` (one path segment shorter than the scoped folder) in the project folder and each folder above it, then in npm's local project folder and each folder above it; on Windows the package is `node_modules\build-os` next to a `buildos.cmd` shim, or in the `node_modules` folder of a `.bin` folder. The rule that the bin file is not inside a `node_modules` folder below the package is relative to the package folder and is unchanged. The `npx` call is `npx -y --prefix <current folder> --workspaces=false build-os@<version>`. The wrapper still never starts a program to learn its version, and a package with any other name, the earlier scoped name too, never counts.
- Release scripts and workflows: `PACKAGE_NAME` in `scripts/release-ledger.ts` (the identity, ledger, SBOM, stage, GitHub, and placeholder checks read it), the tarball paths in `.github/workflows/buildos-release.yml`, the installed-package path in `.github/workflows/buildos-ci.yml`. `.github/CODEOWNERS` names no package and did not change. #### Agent Review (the one review cycle)

- Every counted run exited 0 with `version: 0.1.0`, and every `tarball` digest equalled the reviewed digest. No path or user name is in the record. Install scripts were off. Every non-sacrificable constraint held.
- The first `cold` run (987.7 ms) is the slowest; it is kept, as the profile says. It is the first contact of the pass with the registry (DNS and connection set-up) and is what a first chat session meets; the median is the decision statistic.
- The spread is small for the decision: even the slowest `tarball` run (267.3 ms) is well under the fastest `cold` run (708.0 ms), so the `tarball` share is the smaller part in every repetition.
- Outcome: `pass` (the baseline exists, within the protocol). No finding.

#### Decision (t23)

No package-size reduction is needed now, on the measured machine and network. The reason: the whole first run took under one second there (median 725.6 ms, slowest 987.7 ms), which does not put the protected outcome at risk. Under the profile's decision rule the `tarball` median (261.8 ms) is the smaller part of the `cold` median, so the record recommends no reduction.

The `tarball` workload is a reference measurement, not an upper bound on what a smaller package could save. Its limits (corrected on 2026-11-26 after review round 1 of pull request 5; nothing was measured again):

- The timer in `toolkits/buildos/scripts/measure-npx-first-run.ts` runs from the parent's `spawnSync` call to child exit. So each `tarball` sample also holds the start of its own Node process, DNS, TLS, and the SHA-256 of the bytes, and not only the transfer.
- Inside a cold `npx` run the package size also changes work that the `tarball` workload does not do: unpacking the tarball and writing its 173 files (4,355,182 bytes unpacked) to the npm cache and the install folder.
- So this pass does not say how much a smaller package would save, and it does not split the cold run into a size-dependent part and the rest. The profile's Comparison Method says "the `tarball` share of the cold time is the part a smaller package could shorten"; that is too strong for the reasons above. The profile stays as committed, because its digest is bound to this result; a later `PERF-002` version should say "reference" there.

This sets no target. A slow, metered, or restricted network is outside this scope; it is the `R-012` trial (t17). The decision goes to the owner with the phase closeout.

#### Defect: the Printed Rebuild Command Needs a Global Install (F-P8-11)

Found by review round 1 of pull request 5 on 2026-11-26. The first version of this record said "Defects in the published package: none found by these steps". That was wrong: the steps showed this defect in step 5 and did not check it.

What the adopter sees: in a project made with `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 init`, `entities validate` with no index prints `WARNING [index_stale]: entity-resolution index is missing` and `action: buildos entities rebuild-index --root "<project>" --mode compat --apply`. The JSON result holds the same command in `result.index.remediation_command` and `diagnostics[].correction`. The command is bare `buildos`. An adopter who uses BuildOS through `npx` or the project wrapper has no `buildos` command on `PATH`, so the printed command stops with `buildos: command not found` (exit 127).

Impact: a printed fix command that does not run for an adopter who has no global install. The data and the validation result are correct: `entities validate` exits 0 with `valid: true` in compat mode, and the warning is true. An agent that copies the printed command gets exit 127 and must find the right form itself. With a global install (`npm install -g build-os@0.1.0`, as in the guide's offline install) the bare command runs.

Workarounds (both verified, see the reproduction): `.os/scripts/buildos entities rebuild-index --root <project> --mode compat --apply` (`.os\scripts\buildos.cmd` on Windows, not run in this pass), or `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 entities rebuild-index --root <project> --mode compat --apply`.

Reproduction (verified, macOS 27.2.1 arm64, the official Node 24.22.3 and npm 11.19.1 unpacked into a temporary folder, outside the agent's network sandbox, 2026-11-26). In a new temporary folder with a new empty npm cache (`npm_config_cache=<new empty folder>`), npm's update notice off, stdin closed, and `PATH` set to the Node 24 `bin` folder followed by the standard system command folders only:

| Step | Command (from the project folder) | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `command -v buildos` | prints nothing, exit 1: no `buildos` on `PATH` |
| 2 | `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 init --skip-make-docs` | exit 0 |
| 3 | `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 entities validate --root <project> --mode compat` | exit 0; `action: buildos entities rebuild-index --root "<project>" --mode compat --apply`, and the same text in `remediation_command` |
| 4 | the printed command, run as `sh -c 'buildos entities rebuild-index --root "<project>" --mode compat --apply'` | exit 127, `sh: buildos: command not found` |
| 5 | `.os/scripts/buildos entities rebuild-index --root <project> --mode compat --apply`, on a copy of the project with no index and a new empty npm cache | exit 0, `entities.rebuild-index: ok`, `write status: applied`, stderr empty; then `.os/scripts/buildos entities validate --root <project> --mode compat`: exit 0, no warning |
| 6 | `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 entities rebuild-index --root <project> --mode compat --apply`, on another copy with no index and a new empty npm cache | exit 0, stderr empty; then `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 entities validate --root <project> --mode compat`: exit 0, no warning |

Go baseline: the Go tool printed the same bare command. The Go goldens hold it, for example `toolkits/buildos/test/golden/os/linux/buildos/entities-validate-missing-index-compat-json/stdout` (`"remediation_command": "buildos entities rebuild-index --root \"{ROOT}/root\" --mode compat --apply"` and the same `correction`), and the `rebuildCommand` function in `toolkits/buildos/src/core/entities/commands.ts` is the port of Go `rebuildCommand`. So this is inherited behaviour. In `0.1.0`, adopters run BuildOS through `npx` and the project wrapper, where no `buildos` program needs to be on `PATH`. A fix changes golden output, so it needs a parity exception with an owner decision (`toolkits/buildos/AGENTS.md`: "Output must match the Go goldens byte for byte unless a parity exception with an owner decision says otherwise (`test/golden/parity-exceptions.json`)").

Other printed commands of the same kind (a bare `buildos ...` that BuildOS shows to an adopter as a thing to run), found with `grep` in `toolkits/buildos/src` on 2026-11-26. Not fixed here.

| Where in the source | Printed text | Shown when | Go golden | Tested on `0.1.0` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `src/core/entities/commands.ts:92` (`rebuildCommand`) | `buildos entities rebuild-index --root "<root>" --mode <mode> --apply`, in the human `action:` line, `remediation_command`, and `correction` | `entities validate`, `entities rebuild-index` without `--apply`, and an index failure after `consolidate --apply`, when the index is missing or stale | yes (Go `rebuildCommand`) | yes, smoke step 5: see the reproduction above (exit 127) |
| `src/cli/run.ts:151` | `action: Run buildos help for command syntax.` | an unknown command or a usage error | yes (`test/golden/buildos/cli-unknown-command/stderr`) | yes: `.os/scripts/buildos bogus` printed it, exit 2 |
| `src/cli/help.ts:28` and the usage lines of each domain's help (for example `src/cli/commands/entities.ts:33` to `:36`, `src/cli/commands/validate.ts:26`, `src/cli/commands/version.ts:13`) | `Run "buildos help <domain>" for domain details.` and `buildos <domain> ...` usage lines | `help` and `--help` | the Go help had the same form (`Run "buildos entities help" ...`); the root help text is PE-001 | yes: `.os/scripts/buildos help` printed the line, exit 0 |

The named command was not run. |

The no-TTY `init` question is not in this list: it shows `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 init ...`, which runs. The guide's [chapter 18](../../../guide/content/18-what-is-not-built-yet.md) also names a bare `buildos entities rebuild-index --mode strict --apply` as a workaround; that is guide text, not printed output, and is left for F-P8-11.

Follow-up F-P8-11 (candidate for `0.1.1` or `0.2.0`; owner decision open): the commands that BuildOS prints as a fix use a bare `buildos`, which does not run without a global install. The owner decides whether to fix it, in which release, and in which form (for example the project wrapper form, or the `npx -y build-os@<version>` form), and approves a parity exception for the Go-golden cases (rows 1 and 2 of the table above; row 3 is partly under PE-001). This record does not decide it. Status (owner decision 2026-11-26): fixed in `0.2.0`, with no `0.1.1`; BuildOS prints the fix command as `npx -y build-os@<running version> …`. Disposition for A71: the smoke tests pass on three operating systems as the steps define them (first part met, verified); the steps do not run the printed fix commands, and one of them is the defect F-P8-11 above. That defect is not a difference from the P6 reviewed output (`entities validate` has no P6 capture, and its output equals the Go goldens), so it does not change the output-match count. The second part ("the captured output matches the P6 reviewed output except for version strings") is not met as written: the 5 differences in rows 2, 3, 6a, 8, and 9 are not version strings. Each traces to a later recorded owner decision, phase scope, or review fix, but the criterion is not re-worded. A71 needs the owner to accept these 5 differences, or it stays not met.

### Rollback by Version Pin (t16)

No earlier runnable public version exists: `0.0.0-reserved.0` and `0.0.0-stage` hold no program, and `0.1.0` is the first runnable release. So a rollback through npx to an earlier published version cannot be shown yet, and this record does not fake one.

What was tested instead (verified, macOS, Node 24.22.3, npm 11.19.1, 2026-11-26): an earlier release-candidate version, built locally and never published. In a scratch clone at the source commit `20f941a`, `package.json` was set to `0.0.1-rc.rollback`, then `npm ci --ignore-scripts` and `node scripts/release-build.ts --allow-dirty`: tarball `build-os-0.0.1-rc.rollback.tgz`, SHA-256 `0cad1bf14336ff5b823c9901090083b53f87046fb4de9fb5bcd9b9ed0ecfd82e`, reporting version `0.0.1-rc.rollback` and source revision `20f941a04494ce9c60301cee9e66fab33219a617-dirty`. A project was set up with `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 init --skip-make-docs` and copied (`cp -Rp`); the copy is the test project. The candidate was installed into the copy with `npm install --ignore-scripts --no-save --no-package-lock <tarball>`. Each check ran `sh .os/scripts/buildos version --json`:

| Case | Pin in `.os/manifest.json` | Local install in the copy | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | `0.1.0` | none | version `0.1.0` (through npx), exit 0 |
| B | `0.1.0` | `0.0.1-rc.rollback` | version `0.1.0`, exit 0: the install of another version does not count |
| C | `0.0.1-rc.rollback` (rolled back) | `0.0.1-rc.rollback` | version `0.0.1-rc.rollback`, revision `20f941a...-dirty`, exit 0: the wrapper ran the pinned earlier version; the legacy wrapper `buildos-intake --help` printed its notice and then the help of that version |
| D | the original project, `0.1.0`, untouched | none | version `0.1.0`, exit 0 |
| E | `0.0.1-rc.rollback` | removed | exit 1: npx stops with `npm error code ETARGET` and "No matching version found for build-os@0.0.1-rc.rollback."; the wrapper does not fall back to any other version |
| F | `0.1.0` again (roll forward) | `0.0.1-rc.rollback` still there | version `0.1.0`, exit 0 |

What this proves: on a copied project, the manifest edit alone moves the project wrapper to the pinned version and back, a local npm install counts only when its version equals the pin, and a pin with no matching install and no published version stops instead of running another version. What it does not prove: a rollback to an earlier published version through npx from the registry, which is the path most adopters use, and the Windows `.cmd` wrapper (not run in this pass; the pin-first wrapper tests cover it in CI). So this proves less than A72 asks for the public path, and t16 stays open. Follow-up F-P8-09: prove the public rollback with the second runnable release (`0.2.0` rolling back to `0.1.0`) on a copied project, on the three systems (the smoke workflow can carry the step).

### Offline Install in the Guide (A73, guide part)

The guide documents the offline install: chapter 04, section "Install without access to the npm registry" in `guide/content/04-install-and-configure-your-instance.md` (fetch with `npm pack build-os@0.1.0`, check the SHA-256 against `SECURITY.md` "How to Check a Release", `npm install -g --offline ./build-os-0.1.0.tgz`, then `buildos init`), and "Update and roll back" says how the wrappers use such an install. No guide change was needed.

The documented steps were run (verified, macOS, Node 24.22.3, npm 11.19.1, inside the agent's sandbox): with an empty npm cache and a temporary global prefix, `npm install -g --offline --ignore-scripts ./build-os-0.1.0.tgz` (the registry tarball, SHA-256 `54a8cd01...21e8e`) added 1 package; `buildos init --skip-make-docs` ended "Done. BuildOS is set up in this folder."; `npm_config_offline=true sh .os/scripts/buildos version` printed `version: 0.1.0` (the wrapper ran the installed package, no npx); and `npx -y --offline --package ../build-os-0.1.0.tgz -- buildos version` printed `version: 0.1.0`. This is npm's offline mode, not a restricted network: the restricted-network trial is t17.

### Owner Checklist for t17 (R-012)

t17 needs the maintainer, and no agent did it. Done 2026-11-27 by the owner, owner-reported, without the captures of step 6 and the restricted-network steps: see [Chat-App and Restricted-Network Trials (t17)](#chat-app-and-restricted-network-trials-t17-2026-11-27). These are the exact steps; record the results in a new dated section of this file named "Chat-App and Restricted-Network Trials (t17)", marked owner-reported, with paths and user names replaced as above, and add one dated evidence paragraph to [`R-012`](../../prd/03-open-questions-and-risk-register.md#r-012-node-24-and-npx-reach-in-chat-app-and-enterprise-environments).

Chat-app trial (at least one chat app with folder access that adopters use):

1. On a computer with Node.js 24 or newer, run `node --version` and `npm --version` in a terminal and note both.
2. Make a new empty folder. Give the chat app access to that folder only.
3. Ask the agent, word for word: "In this folder, run `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 init`. If BuildOS asks a question, ask me, then run the command it prints."
4. Answer "no" to the Make Docs question (or "yes", and note which).
5. Then ask: "Run `.os/scripts/buildos validate` in this folder." (On Windows: `.os\scripts\buildos.cmd validate`.)
6. Capture: the chat app name and version; the operating system; whether the agent could start `npx` at all (sandbox or permission prompts, and what you approved); the full text the agent got from each command, with its exit code when shown; about how long the first command took before any output, and whether at any point you thought it had failed or hung; whether the agent asked you the Make Docs question; and the folder after: the list of top-level names and the text of `.os/manifest.json`.

Restricted-network trial (once, on a network that blocks or proxies `registry.npmjs.org`, for example a company network or a firewall rule):

1. Run `npm view build-os@0.1.0 version` and `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 version` in a new empty folder with a new empty npm cache (`npm_config_cache=<new empty folder>`). Capture the exact error text, the exit code, and about how long each took to fail.
2. Follow guide chapter 04, "Install without access to the npm registry", steps 1 to 4, with the tarball fetched on a machine with access. The SHA-256 must be `54a8cd01f0165226927a74e5108dd37327323bd3db1905fdb6323c7373b21e8e`; capture the `shasum` (or `certutil`) line.
3. In a new empty folder: `buildos init --skip-make-docs`, then `.os/scripts/buildos version` (Windows: `.os\scripts\buildos.cmd version`). Capture the output and exit codes, and whether any command tried to reach the registry.

Where the result goes: the new section named above (the facts, marked owner-reported), the `R-012` evidence paragraph (one paragraph with the date and a link to that section), and the t17 line of [08 Release 0.1.0](08-release-0-1-0.md#stage-4---staged-package-proof). `R-012` closes only when its "To close" text is met: tested in the chat apps adopters use, including at least one restricted network, and the offline install documented. Update 2026-11-27: the owner closed `R-012` by owner decision on the trials below ([Chat-App and Restricted-Network Trials (t17)](#chat-app-and-restricted-network-trials-t17-2026-11-27)).

### Chat-App and Restricted-Network Trials (t17) (2026-11-27)

Owner-reported. The owner (Tyler) did these trials on 2026-11-27 with the [Owner Checklist for t17 (R-012)](#owner-checklist-for-t17-r-012) and reported the results in the orchestrator's chat the same day. No agent ran or saw them. This section holds what the owner reported, and only that.

| Trial | What the owner reported |
| --- | --- |
| Chat-app trial | Done in the ChatGPT/Codex chat app. Everything went as expected, and the outputs were what the build should give. One thing was noteworthy: the very first time the `npx` command ran, it took about 1 minute and 18 seconds before the chat appeared to run the command again; the (apparent) second time, the agent read the output almost immediately. The chat app hides most command output from the user. |
| Restricted-network trial | Done. Everything went as expected. It did not appear that any command tried to reach the registry. |

The owner states that it is not feasible for the owner to capture the actual output and exit codes. Not captured, so not in this report:

- Chat-app trial: the chat app's version; the operating system; the `node --version` and `npm --version` output; whether the agent could start `npx` at once, and which sandbox or permission prompts appeared and what was approved; the full command text that the agent ran and the full text that the agent got from each command, with exit codes; whether the agent asked the Make Docs question, and the answer; the folder listing after `init`, and the text of `.os/manifest.json`; the output of `.os/scripts/buildos validate`.
- Restricted-network trial: the kind of network and how it blocks or proxies the registry; the operating system and the Node.js and npm versions; the exact error text, the exit code, and the time to fail of `npm view build-os@0.1.0 version` and `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 version`; the `shasum` (or `certutil`) line of the tarball; the output and exit codes of `buildos init --skip-make-docs` and `.os/scripts/buildos version`.

The first run of about 78 seconds is an observation, and its cause is not established. The first `npx -y build-os@0.1.0` run downloads the package. The measured first run of `PERF-002` on the maintainer's machine and network had a median of 725.6 ms ([First-Run npx (PERF-002, P8)](#first-run-npx-perf-002-p8)), under one second. The chat app's own handling of the command (its sandbox, approvals, time limits, or a retry) was not visible to the owner. So this report does not say whether the time was spent in npm, in the network, or in the chat app. The `PERF-002` profile names this trial as a next review condition ([PERF-002 Profile](08-release-0-1-0.md#perf-002-profile)); that profile has expired for `0.2.0` anyway, and its new version comes before the `0.2.0` measurement (runbook step k).

What this meets. A73 ("The evidence report records the chat-app and restricted-network results, and the guide documents the offline install"): met by its words. This section records both results, and the guide documents the offline install ([Offline Install in the Guide (A73, guide part)](#offline-install-in-the-guide-a73-guide-part)). The results are owner-reported and have none of the detailed captures that the checklist asks for; A73's words do not ask for captures. t17 ("Run `buildos init` through at least one chat app with folder access that adopters use, and once on a restricted network. Record the results for `R-012`."): done as an owner-reported trial. Its checkbox stays unticked, because Stage 4 does not pass (A72 is open until step k).

`R-012`, as first recorded: it stays open. Its "To close" text is: "BuildOS is tested in the chat apps adopters use, including at least one restricted network, and the offline install is documented." The restricted network and the offline install are covered. "The chat apps adopters use" is plural, and one chat app was tried, owner-reported, without captures, so closing `R-012` is a judgement call for the owner, not for an agent. Owner question: is the one owner-reported trial in the ChatGPT/Codex chat app enough to close `R-012` (A), or does `R-012` stay open until a trial in each other chat app that adopters use is recorded (B)? The implementer and the orchestrator recommended B (keep it open). `R-012` is not a step 0 item, so this question does not hold the `0.2.0` release.

Owner decision 2026-11-27, later the same day: "I think we can close it now." `R-012` is closed in the register ([`R-012`](../../prd/03-open-questions-and-risk-register.md#r-012-node-24-and-npx-reach-in-chat-app-and-enterprise-environments), Resolution). The owner closed it knowing that the recommendation was to keep it open. The closing rests on this evidence only: one chat-app trial (ChatGPT/Codex), owner-reported, without captures; one restricted-network trial, owner-reported, without captures; and the offline install, documented in guide chapter 04 and tested in npm's offline mode on macOS on 2026-11-26 ([Offline Install in the Guide (A73, guide part)](#offline-install-in-the-guide-a73-guide-part)). No other chat app was tried. The first run of about 78 seconds stays recorded above as an observation whose cause is not established.

### Question for t25

t25 stays for the maintainer, and no agent ticks it. To close t25 by the dated exception of 2026-11-26, the owner answers one question:

> Do you accept the retrospective publication review of 2026-11-26 for `build-os@0.1.0` (the section above) as the publication approval of `0.1.0`: yes or no?

What stays missed whatever the answer: A75's order. The review was not approved before publication, so for `0.1.0` "publication happens only after a recorded maintainer approval" is recorded as missed, and a later review cannot meet it. A "yes" closes t25 by the explicit exception, and the record must say so; it does not make A75 met. A "no" leaves t25 open and asks for an owner decision on `0.1.0` (for example a `0.1.1`, or deprecating `0.1.0`).

Answered 2026-11-27 (owner decision): "Yes". The owner answered after the orchestrator showed the owner the review above. So t25 is closed by the explicit dated exception, and A75's order stays recorded as missed for `0.1.0`. A75 is not met. The t25 checkbox stays unticked under the rule in [00-index.md](00-index.md), because Stage 5 does not pass (A75). See [Owner Decisions of 2026-11-27](#owner-decisions-of-2026-11-27-020-release).

### Follow-ups (Post-Publication Checks)

- F-P8-09: prove rollback by version pin through npx to an earlier published version (`0.2.0` back to `0.1.0`) on a copied project, on three systems, when `0.2.0` exists. Owner: the `0.2.0` release phase.
- F-P8-10: on Windows, the shown `entities` remediation command doubles each backslash (Go `%q` parity). Check that Command Prompt runs it as shown, and decide whether a parity exception is wanted. Status (2026-11-26): fixed for `0.2.0` in PE-023; see [F-P8-11 Printed Commands](#f-p8-11-printed-commands-2026-11-26).
- F-P8-11: the commands that BuildOS prints as a fix use a bare `buildos` (first `entities rebuild-index`; also `buildos help`, `buildos validate`, `buildos init`, and the three legacy-name notices in their messages), which exits 127 for an adopter with no global install. Candidate for `0.1.1` or `0.2.0`; owner decision open, with a parity exception for the Go-golden cases. See [Defect: the Printed Rebuild Command Needs a Global Install (F-P8-11)](#defect-the-printed-rebuild-command-needs-a-global-install-f-p8-11).
- F-P8-12: `toolkits/buildos/scripts/measure-npx-first-run.ts` does not pin the child `PATH` to the Node that runs the script, so the BuildOS CLI that `npx` starts could run under another Node (the script starts `npx` itself with the Node that runs the script). For the `PERF-002` pass of 2026-11-26 the raw JSON records Node 24.22.3 and the launch command put that Node first on `PATH`, so the result stands. Pin the child `PATH` in the next revision of the instrument. Status (2026-11-26): fixed in W1 R7 P9 Stage 3; see [P9 Stage 3](#p9-stage-3-skills-no-python-check-and-docs-2026-11-26).
- F-P8-13: `toolkits/buildos/scripts/published-smoke.ts` cleans paths before it checks the legacy notice, so an account named `buildos` on the machine could make a correct notice fail the check. The three CI smoke jobs passed. Compare the raw stderr first, then clean the saved report. Status (2026-11-26): fixed in W1 R7 P9 Stage 3; see [P9 Stage 3](#p9-stage-3-skills-no-python-check-and-docs-2026-11-26).

## P9 Skill-Script Commands

On 2026-11-24, W1 R7 P9 Stage 1 (script goldens, t1 to t3) and Stage 2 (commands, t4 to t8) were built on the branch `rewrite/ts-cli-p9` from `38d1e08`, on macOS arm64 with Node 26.13.1 and Python 3.14.10 (for the capture only). Nothing was pushed, merged, published, staged, tagged, or released. The package version stays `0.0.0-dev`, and `release-candidates.json` is unchanged.

Commit hashes and branch names in the P9 sections of this report, in the P9 history records, and in the P9 test and golden files (for example `38d1e08`, `576d9ce`, and the branches `rewrite/ts-cli-p9` to `rewrite/ts-cli-p9-owner4`) name commits and branches of the earlier history, which exists only in the private archive repository `brucewaynedecoy/build-os-archive`: the public repository starts from one clean commit (owner decision of 2026-11-25). The P9 Stage 1 and Stage 2 work came into the public repository on 2026-11-26 as file content only; see [P9 Move to the Public Repository](#p9-move-to-the-public-repository-2026-11-26).

### Order Departure

The phase entry gate is "P8 exit gate passed". P8 waits on owner actions, so the orchestrator started Stages 1 and 2 early, implementation only, on a separate branch, so that the `0.1.0` release candidate on `rewrite/ts-cli` does not gain the `0.2.0` commands. This is a recorded departure from the default arc. Stage 3 (skill updates and script deletion, the no-Python CI check, the CI image without Python, the guide and README, and the release) is not started and waits for the P8 exit gate.

### Capture Record (t2)

`toolkits/buildos/test/golden/skills/capture.ts` writes the goldens (`test/golden/skills/<script>/cases/<case>.json`, and the workbooks openpyxl wrote in `test/golden/skills/fitgap/xlsx/`), and `--check` compares and writes nothing:

```sh
node test/golden/skills/capture.ts --python <venv>/bin/python            # all three scripts
node test/golden/skills/capture.ts --check --script fitgap --python <venv>/bin/python
```

It reads each script from git at `38d1e08` (`git show`) and refuses one whose SHA-256 differs from `test/golden/skills/script-sha256.json`: `work.py` `1ab581af…e1b5`, `fitgap.py` `796aca12…88e6`, `azure_boards_csv.mjs` `e5f3b616…0318`, `adapters/dynamics-365-ce.mjs` `5f20eea0…f5d4`. `capture-record.json` names Python 3.14.10 (`-P -s`, `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`, `TZ=UTC`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8`), openpyxl 3.1.5 and et_xmlfile 2.0.0 with the SHA-256 of each one's installed `RECORD` file (`42867ad4…1f45`, `137ac111…85c6`), Node v26.13.1, `darwin arm64`, and the clock. The openpyxl copy came from the local uv cache into a throwaway virtual environment under the temporary folder (the network check for PyPI failed in the sandbox); nothing was installed globally or committed.

Determinism: the scripts embed the time (`work.py` time stamps, `fitgap.py` `--date`), so a small runner fixes the clock at `2026-01-15T12:00:00Z` (it replaces `datetime.datetime.now` for `work.py` and `datetime.date.today` for `fitgap.py`, then runs the script with `runpy`); BuildOS gets the same clock through `RunOptions.now`. `work.py` writes the keys of a Python set, whose order changes with each run's hash seed, so the capture fixes `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` (divergence SD-08). Normalizations: N1 the project folder (as given and resolved) becomes `<root>`, and on Windows a `\` after `<root>` in BuildOS output becomes `/`; N2 a Python traceback keeps its last line; N3 a workbook is recorded by its SHA-256 and compared by content; N4 the fixed clock. `--check` passed for all three scripts after the final capture (openpyxl writes the current time into each workbook, so `--check` compares workbooks by content).

### The `.xlsx` Rule (t3, proposed PE-021)

`test/xlsx-compare.ts` reads both workbooks with the repository's own reader, `src/core/fitgap/xlsx-read.ts` (the port of Go's `encoding/xml` and the intake ZIP reader, extended for styles, tables, links, and conditional formats), and compares content. Proposed parity exception PE-021 in `test/golden/proposed-exceptions.json`, pending an owner decision (A76), says:

> Skill-script parity for a .xlsx file compares workbook content, not archive bytes: buildos fitgap workbook writes its own Office Open XML parts (zipped with the bundled fflate), and the fitgap.py script wrote them with openpyxl, so the bytes always differ. Equal are the sheet names and order and the opening sheet; every cell that has a value or a style, with its value and type (text, number, boolean, formula), font (bold, italic, underline, size, color), solid fill color, alignment (vertical, wrap), and number format; merged cells, column widths, row heights, and frozen panes; internal links; tables (name, range, columns, style, row stripes); conditional formats (range, type, priority, operator, formula, the format's fill and font color, color-scale and data-bar points and colors); the landscape fit-to-width page setup; and the document title and creator. Not compared: archive bytes, ZIP times and entry order, XML spelling, style and string indexes, the color alpha byte (openpyxl writes 00, BuildOS FF), the document times (BuildOS writes the fixed 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z), the application name, and parts the skill does not set.

A difference is reported by sheet, cell, and field only, never a cell value (`test/xlsx-compare.test.ts` shows it). All six workbook steps compare equal.

Update 2026-11-25: the owner approved PE-021 as written, and it moved to `test/golden/parity-exceptions.json`. See [P9 Owner Decisions 2026-11-25](#p9-owner-decisions-2026-11-25).

## P9 CI Run 45535678445

The first three-OS CI run of `4c02048` (`rewrite/ts-cli-p9`) failed 25 tests on Ubuntu, macOS, and Windows (Node 24): the 14 fit-gap parity cases, the 3 workbook structure tests, and 8 fit-gap hostile and envelope tests. Every other test passed, the `extract bulk` and `export azure-boards` parity cases too, so Node 24 prints the same `JSON.parse` messages as Node 26.13.1, which captured the goldens (P9-O3 closed: no normalization rule is needed).

Cause (finding P9-R1-09): the root `.gitignore` rule `build/` matched `toolkits/buildos/test/fixtures/skills/fitgap/bases/library/build/`, so the 36 files the fixture generator wrote there were never committed. The local runs passed because the files were on disk.

Fix (`f364ee3`): the fixture folder is `analysis/`; the generator, the cases, the 14 fit-gap goldens (captured again with the scripts at `38d1e08`; only the folder name and the time openpyxl writes into a workbook changed), the SD-03 pins, and the tests use it. No ignore rule changed. `test/fixture-tracking.test.ts` asks git whether any file under `test/fixtures/` or `test/golden/` matches an ignore rule (`git check-ignore --no-index`) and shows that the old folder would be caught; it skips with a reason outside a git checkout. The decisive check, a fresh `git archive` of the final commit, is in [Check Results (P9 Review Round 1)](#check-results-p9-review-round-1).

## P9 CI Run 45542114946

The three-OS CI run of `9f5aee9` (`rewrite/ts-cli-p9`, review round 1) passed on Ubuntu and macOS (Node 24). On Windows the three skill-parity suites passed, and one test failed: `P9-R1-13: a typed path follows the shared layout rule` in `test/skill-script-review.test.ts`.

Cause (finding P9-R2-03): the test searched the `validate` report for `\system\csv\good.csv` with single backslashes, but the report is JSON, which writes each Windows backslash as two. The command was right; the test was wrong. Fix (`7df73a1`): the test parses the report and compares its `input` field with `join(dir, "system", "csv", "good.csv")`. The neighboring test named "the same for a fit-gap output and an emit output" ran only `fitgap`; it now also runs `export azure-boards emit` with a `system/` output and checks the written file and the reported output path. Every P9 test file was read again for separator assumptions: paths that a command reports are compared after `JSON.parse` or as the port's `/` form, typed paths are built with `join`, and the round 2 tests use a junction for a folder link on Windows. A three-OS run of the fix branch is still needed (nothing was pushed).

## P9 Review Round 2

On 2026-11-25 the findings of the second independent review, of `9f5aee9`, were fixed on the branch `rewrite/ts-cli-p9-fix2` (from `9f5aee9`) in `7df73a1`, on macOS arm64 with Node 26.13.1. Each finding was checked against the code first; none was wrong. Each fix has a test that fails without it: the 33 tests of the new `test/skill-script-review-2.test.ts`, run against the source of `9f5aee9` (with a one-line export of its old `fnmatchRegex` so the file loads), fail 32 of 33; the one that passes is the control test that a path really outside the project is still exit 3. The P9-R2-03 change fixes a test, not the code, so the corrected test passes on both. As the reviewer asked, write faults are injected before a port call and after it took effect: the test port lets the rename happen and then throws as the adapter does when the folder flush fails (an `FsWriteFailure` at `sync-parent` that carries `WriteLeftovers.committed`), and one test uses the real adapter's `sync-parent` hook on POSIX. Nothing was pushed, merged, published, staged, tagged, or released.

### Findings and Dispositions (P9 Round 2)

| ID | Disposition | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P9-R2-01 | Fixed. `BulkFs.apply` journals the port's `committed` entry of a failed write before the undo runs, so a requirement file renamed into place is put back. Each undo of a path expects the entry the later step put back (round 1's undo failed on the second of two writes of one file, the review's intent and its final state). The undo stops at the first file it cannot put back for sure: an earlier file put back whose folder flush failed is `unsure`, so the publication intent stays while any data file of the publication is not surely back, and the report is exit 10, `partially_applied`, with every path and reason. The resume was already idempotent by the recorded before and after hashes. Every mutating bulk command goes through `apply`; `start`, `stage`, `stage-update`, `replace-row`, and `decide` each get a fault after their first write took effect. The shared writer got the same audit (P9-R2-07) | `skill-script-review-2.test.ts` P9-R2-01 (9 tests: undo complete, undo incomplete with the intent kept and a retry with one copy, the final review write, the real adapter hook, and the five other commands) |
| P9-R2-02 | Fixed (inherited script defect). `fitgap packages` removes only a `pkg-*.json` that has a numbered name as it writes them (`pkg-01.json` to `pkg-99.json`, then `pkg-100.json` and up), is a regular file, and is UTF-8 JSON with exactly the fields of a package item, in order (each requirement too). It reads each such file once, at most 128 MiB, with no link followed, through the destination's own port (`ProjectFiles.readDestination`). Every other `pkg-*.json` is kept and named on stderr and in `result.kept`. ### Evidence Wording Corrected (Final Check)

- SD-05 and SD-20 (file preservation): round 2 said every `pkg-*.json` that BuildOS did not write "is kept"; a kept file at a name the run wrote was then replaced. Now exactly true: a kept file is never written over, because the run stops before any change when one is at a name it writes.

It now also compares the one score-driving model field, so a stale priority cannot reach the workbook. It still records no content fingerprint, so a change to a field that does not drive the score (a name or a summary) builds a workbook with the new text, as the script did.
- The recovery message: round 2 said "the review still holds the pending publication" whenever the review was among the paths not put back; it now says what the review holds.

### The Intake Envelope (PE-022)

The intake commands use the rules of PE-011 (`src/cli/commands/go-tool.ts`), the same as `discovery` and `design`:

- `--json` counts only as a whole argument in flag position of the subcommand. `-json`, `--json=true`, `--source --json`, `-- --json`, and `--json` before the subcommand behave as in Go.
- `command` is `intake.convert`, `intake.index.references`, or `intake.index.playbooks`. `root` is `--repo-root` as Go cleans it, or empty when the flags did not parse.
- `write_status` is `planned` for a dry run, `applied` for a write, and `not_requested` for a failure.
- `result` for `convert`: `outputs` (each with `path`, `source`, `type`, `status`, `sha256`), `side_artifacts`, `warnings`, and `dry_run`. For an index: `output_path` and `count`.
- A conversion warning (an image BuildOS did not copy) is a `warning` diagnostic, `image_not_copied`, and not a stderr line.
- A failure has `ok` false, `result` null, and one error diagnostic: `usage_error` for a flag or usage error, `command_failed` for a Go error, or the core code of a refusal.
- stdout holds only the envelope, and stderr is empty. The exit code is the one of the text form: 0; 1 for a Go or usage error, as the Go tool; 3 for a write outside the root.
- Help and the usage text stay the Go text (PE-001, PE-002), so the usage text does not list `--json`.
- Without `--json`, the output is the Go text, byte for byte.

One fix came with it: `usageFailure` in `go-tool.ts` now keeps the switches already found, so `intake convert --json` without `--source` prints the envelope. For `discovery` and `design`, it is called only before the flags are parsed, so their output does not change.

On 2026-11-25 the findings of the independent review of the intake `--json` envelope (`4705e52` and `e07b993`, PE-022) were fixed on the branch `rewrite/ts-cli-p9-owner2` (from `e07b993`), on macOS arm64 with Node 26.13.1. The orchestrator accepted all eight findings. Each code fix has a test in `toolkits/buildos/test/intake-json.test.ts` that fails without it: the new test file, run against the source of `e07b993` (a `git archive` extract), fails 10 of 21 tests. The failures are the seven tests for findings 1 to 5 and the three success tests with the new path form. Finding 6 and finding 7 change text only, and the strengthened text test of finding 8 passes on both, because the text form did not change. ### Findings and Dispositions (Intake JSON Round 1)

| Finding | What changed | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (major) A partial conversion reported `not_requested` | With `--json`, `intake convert` and `intake index` keep a write log (`WriteLog` in `src/core/intake/io.ts`): each folder that `MkdirAll` makes and each new file, with its identity right after the write, and each earlier file that a write changed (`--force`). After a failed write, the log removes, newest first, each folder and file this run made, only while it is still that entry, and never an entry that was there before. A complete undo gives `not_requested` and the failure's exit code. When something stays, the envelope has `partially_applied`, `result.not_restored` (path, reason, `state`), one `undo_incomplete` diagnostic per entry, and exit 10, in the form of `extract bulk` and `fitgap` (`skill-output.ts`). Without `--json`, nothing is undone, as in Go (exit 1). PE-022, PRD 20, `SECURITY.md`, and register `D-010` say how the two modes differ | Finding 1 (3 tests): disk full on the second write of the workbook fixture (JSON: everything this run made is gone and `assets/.gitkeep` stays; text: Go's files stay); a folder that another program filled during the run (exit 10, `assets/inventory/`, the foreign file kept); `--force` over earlier twins (exit 10, both replaced paths named; text form exit 1); an index write into new folders |
| 2 (major) An unexpected error printed two forms | `fail` in `go-tool.ts` reports an unexpected error itself, in the mode the leaf parser decided and with the leaf's root: the envelope with an `internal_error` diagnostic and nothing on stderr, or the dispatcher's line `buildos: internal error: <first line>` (exit 1). The dispatcher no longer sees the error, so it never scans the raw arguments again. This also applies to `discovery` and `design`, which use the same `fail`; their text form is unchanged | Finding 2: a port fault with `--json` gives only the envelope, with the project root (not `/`); with `--source --json`, `--json` after a positional argument, or after `--`, only the text line |
