Each code fix has a test in `toolkits/buildos/test/intake-json.test.ts` or `toolkits/buildos/test/fs-port.test.ts` that fails without it: the two test files, run against the source of `4f4fb08` (a `git archive` extract), fail 11 of 151 tests, which are the 9 new tests and the 2 extended round 2 tests (finding 4). Text output without `--json` is the same, byte for byte, in every case that has no race, and every Go parity golden passes. Nothing was pushed, merged, published, staged, tagged, or released.

### Findings and Dispositions (Intake JSON Final Check)

| Finding | What changed | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (major) Without `--force`, the writer could truncate a twin or side artifact that another program made after the last existence check | Go had the same race: its `writeConvertedOutput` and `writeSideArtifact` call `os.Stat`, then `os.WriteFile` (`O_TRUNC`), at the baseline `263f5ca`. The fix stays. `writeFileInPlace` takes `InPlaceWriteOptions` (`src/core/shared/fs-port.ts`). With `overwrite: false`, the adapter (`src/adapters/node-fs.ts`) never opens an entry at the name, and an `O_EXCL` collision is not tried again as an overwrite; it throws `FsWriteFailure` (step `open`, `EEXIST`). `IntakeFs.writeFileWithParents` (`src/core/intake/io.ts`) takes the Go error text, and `writeConvertedOutput` and `writeSideArtifact` (`convert.ts`) pass it without `--force`, so the collision gives `output exists, use --force to overwrite: <path>` or `side artifact exists, ...` (exit 1) and the other file keeps its bytes. With `--json`, the folders the run made before the collision are listed (exit 10). The racing case differs from Go (Go overwrote and exited 0); PE-010 now states it. `--force` and the index commands keep the overwrite | `fs-port.test.ts`: an entry at the check and an entry made before the `O_EXCL` open are both `EEXIST` and `untouched`, the bytes stay; the default still overwrites. `intake-json.test.ts` (2 tests): a twin made after the existence check, and a side artifact made just before the exclusive create, in the text form (exit 1, Go's text) and with `--json` (exit 10, the run's folders listed) |
| 2 (major) A refusal of the writer factory (`openWriter`) gave exit 10 and listed the absent file as `changed` | `writeFileWithParents` opens the writer (`binding.inPlace()`) before the `try` that records effects, so a factory refusal is not taken as an untagged write error | A factory that throws `PathRefusedError` for `intake index playbooks` with an existing output folder: text exit 3; JSON exit 3, `not_requested`, `result` null, one diagnostic, no file |
| 3 (major) An open failure after the writer removed an index link said the index was overwritten and its content lost | The adapter tags the error (`withInPlaceEffect(error, effect, linkRemoved)`, `inPlaceLinkRemovedOf`). `WriteChange.link` carries it; the diagnostic says that the run removed the link at the path, that the file the link pointed to is not changed, and to make the link again. The entry stays `changed`, exit 10 | POSIX only (a link): `.os/indexes/references.json` a link to `real.json`, an injected `EACCES` at the open: exit 10, `changed`, the link diagnostic, `real.json` unchanged, the link gone |
| 4 (major) The recovery text could make an operator delete another program's replacement | The `created` text now says what the run did at that time and that another program can have changed the path after that. The correction says to look at the entry that is at the path now before removing anything. `SECURITY.md` qualifies the ownership statement: a listed path is not proof that BuildOS owns the entry there now | The round 2 test "a file that another program put in place" now asserts the diagnostic and the correction; the round 2 disk-full test asserts the new text |
| 5 (minor) On a case-insensitive volume, `image1.png` and `IMAGE1.PNG` with `--force` were listed twice | The writer already has the identity of the opened file (its `fstat` right after the open; an inode of 0 is no identity). It gives it through `InPlaceWriteOptions.opened`, with no new lookup. `WriteRecord` skips a file write whose identity an earlier write of the run opened, so the first spelling and reason stay; distinct files keep distinct identities | `fs-port.test.ts`: one file gives one identity, two files two. `intake-json.test.ts`: a `.docx` with both media names, `--force`, a failure at the twin: one `created` image entry on a case-insensitive volume, two on a case-sensitive one (the test checks the volume). On Linux CI, the end-to-end test also passes on the old code; the adapter test covers the identity there |
| 6 (minor) No deterministic close fault after a successful write | A test hook `writeRaceHooks.afterStep` (`close-in-place`) runs right after the in-place writer's real close; a test throws from it | `fs-port.test.ts`: step `close`, `EIO`, `created` for a new file and `changed` for an existing one, the bytes complete. `intake-json.test.ts`: an index write with the close fault gives exit 10, `created`, a `close ...` message, then `changed` on the next run |
| 7 (minor) PRD 20 and PE-022 promised equal exit codes and also said a partial write exits 1 in text mode | PRD 20 and PE-022 now say: the text form keeps the exit code of the underlying failure (1 for a failed write, 3 for a refusal); with `--json`, a failure after a recorded change exits 10, also when the text form gives another code (an index whose parent folder the run made before the port refused the file: 3 and 10). PRD 20 has a requirement history entry | Text only |

### Departures and Notes (Stage 3)

- Order: Stage 3 ran before the P8 exit gate (orchestrator decision, recorded in the entry gate).

The job does not remove it; it runs every check with a `PATH` that finds no Python, and proves that on each of the three systems. A Linux container image without Python was not used, so no Docker image digest had to be pinned. A program that names an absolute path could still reach Python; the three commands start no program at all (in `src/`, only `init` loads the process adapter).
- t12 "draft `0.2.0` release notes": the brief said not to write the final notes or set the version. The phase file asks for a draft, so `RELEASE_NOTES.md` has a section marked draft; the version and the final text are t13.
- `test/skill-script-parity.test.ts` counts a file the golden step removed (state `null`) as equal to a file BuildOS did not touch (`stateEqual`, `a ?? null`). So in `fitgap/packages` step 1 the golden's removal of the stale `pkg-09.json` and BuildOS keeping it (SD-20) compare equal. SD-20 approves that difference, so no result is wrong, but the parity test would not see an unapproved removal difference either. The smoke script follows the same rule. New follow-up F-P9-07; the parity test was not changed.
- The smoke script compares exit codes and written files, not text, because it runs with the real clock: in `bulk-extract/replace-and-decide` step 17 (`decide`), BuildOS rewrites the review file in some runs and not in others, because the time it writes can equal the one the step before wrote (5 of 8 local runs). The parity test, with its fixed clock, compares the text and the files byte for byte.

### A80: a Linux Image Without Python

A80 reads "Each command runs successfully in the CI image without Python." The job `no-python-image` gives it that image for Linux:

- Image: the official `node:24-slim` image (Debian bookworm, Node.js 24.22.3, npm 11), image index digest `sha256:873f586f3794f52281bd039bf02c048a0be08fde619338f9941bad1eb6b34530`, built 2026-11-24 (its linux/amd64 manifest is `sha256:e0e989b967dacc279681ed81774b2ce9eeebbb0efb8e0c427573235bebf1eda1`). The workflow pulls it by that digest, as it pins actions by commit SHA, and `SECURITY.md` (CI Checks) records the image and the digest; `test/check-no-python.test.ts` fails when the two differ or when the image is not pinned by digest. A new digest is a reviewed change to both.
- How it runs: `docker run --rm` on `ubuntu-latest`, with only the checkout mounted, running `toolkits/buildos/scripts/no-python-image.sh` with `sh -eu`. It is not a job container, because GitHub mounts the runner's tool cache, which holds Python, into a job container, and the search would find it there.
- What it runs, with the image's own `PATH`: the dependency guards before and after `npm ci --ignore-scripts`, the no-Python check, the build, the pack, a new project (`buildos init --skip-make-docs`) with the tarball installed (`--offline --ignore-scripts`), `scripts/no-python-smoke.ts`, and `test/skill-script-parity.test.ts`. The smoke is the same one as in the `no-python` job: the `PATH` proof, the skills' commands through the project wrapper (both skill CSVs byte for byte), and the 61 fixture cases.
- The filesystem proof: with `--filesystem / --skip <checkout>`, the smoke first searches every entry of the container filesystem, without following links, except the checkout, `/proc`, `/sys`, and `/dev`. A Python that can run stops the run with exit 1: a file with an execute bit, or a link, named `py` or starting with `python` or `pypy` (an interpreter or its launcher); a `libpython*` file or link (the interpreter library); a folder named `python` or `pypy` followed by a digit (a standard library folder such as `python3.11`). So does a folder it cannot read. Any other entry with such a name, and every `.py` source file, is listed, not failed on: a source file or a data folder is not a Python that can run. The first CI run of the job (run 45920836350) used a stricter rule, any entry with such a name, and failed on `/usr/share/gcc/python`: a folder of GDB helper sources (`.py` files for the debugger) that Debian's C++ library package `libstdc++6` installs. It holds no interpreter, so the rule now lists it. The search runs after the installs, so it covers the image and everything installed into it.
- What the slim image lacks: git. Nothing in the script needs it: the checkout is made on the runner, the smoke and the parity test read no git history, and `test/capture-sources.test.ts`, which needs git and the full history, runs in the `test` job (on all three systems). Nothing installs Python or any other package.
- Checked before CI: the Node.js 24.22.3 linux-x64 release tarball (the files the image adds to Debian) lists 5,888 entries with no Python name and 59 `.py` files (58 in npm's node-gyp, 1 in `share/doc/node`). The image's build steps install no Python package. Docker is not on this machine, so the job itself ran only in CI.

The `no-python` job is unchanged: on macOS and Windows (and Ubuntu) the hosted runner images have Python installed, and that job proves only that the commands find none on the `PATH` it gives them.

Wording for A80 (the criterion's text is unchanged): A80 is met for Linux by the image: each command runs in the `node:24-slim` image, which holds no Python at all. For macOS and Windows it is met by the restricted `PATH`: the commands run with no Python on `PATH`, on runner images that do have Python. The words of A80 ask for "the CI image without Python" and do not name the three systems, so this round claims it on that reading. If the owner reads A80 as an image without Python on all three systems, it is not met for macOS and Windows, and no hosted image without Python exists for them. Status: met, by [CI run 45921131235](#ci-run-of-bf6db38-stage-3-review-round-1) of `bf6db38`.

### Upgrade Test (Finding 2)

Reproduction (macOS, the published `build-os@0.1.0` from the registry): `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 init --root . --skip-make-docs` in a new folder; then `.os/skills/` replaced by this branch's `system/.os/skills/`; then `.os/scripts/buildos extract bulk status --root .` printed `ERROR [usage_error]: unknown command "extract"` with `version: 0.1.0`, exit 2. The pin in `.os/manifest.json` was still `0.1.0`, and the wrapper always runs the pinned version.

`buildos init` on an existing project: `0.2.0` (the local build below) run in that `0.1.0` project with `--skip-make-docs` exited 0 with "BuildOS is already set up in this folder, and its sections are up to date. Nothing was changed." The pin stayed `0.1.0` and the `0.1.0` skill scripts stayed in `.os/skills/`. This is the designed rerun (`src/core/init/plan.ts`: a rerun writes no file of its own and only refreshes a BuildOS section of a shared file; W2 owns update). So `init` is not the refresh tool, and the product has no update command. The steps use `init` only in a new, empty folder, where it is the supported way to get the `0.2.0` skills.

What changes between `0.1.0` and `0.2.0` in a project: `git diff v0.1.0 HEAD -- system/` changes only files under `system/.os/skills/` (14 files: 5 deleted, 9 changed). The wrappers, contracts, templates, config, and data files are the same, so the steps refresh only the pin and the skills. This is to check again at t13, against the final `0.2.0` tree.

How `0.2.0` was simulated (it is not published): a copy of this working tree (no `.git`, no `node_modules`) with `version` set to `0.2.0` in the copy's `toolkits/buildos/package.json`, built with `BUILDOS_RELEASE_VERSION=0.2.0` and packed: `build-os-0.2.0.tgz`, 168 files, `buildos version` prints `version: 0.2.0`. This repository's version is unchanged. Where the steps run `npx -y build-os@0.2.0`, the test ran `npx -y --package=<build-os-0.2.0.tgz> -- buildos`, which runs the same bin from the file. The wrapper's `npx` fallback cannot be simulated without a registry: with the pin at `0.2.0` and no install, it stops with `npm error notarget No matching version found for build-os@0.2.0` (exit 1), as expected before publication. So the test installed the tarball into the project's `node_modules` (`npm install --offline --ignore-scripts --no-save`), which the wrapper uses as an npm install of exactly the pinned version.

The steps, on a new `0.1.0` project in git, with a copy of `buildos-bulk-extract` in `.claude/skills/` as an app install:

| Step | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Set `buildos_version` to `0.2.0` in `.os/manifest.json` | One line changed |
| 2. `init --root . --skip-make-docs` with `0.2.0` in a new, empty folder outside the project | exit 0 |
| 3. Delete `.os/skills/`, copy the new one in its place | `git status`: the five script files deleted, 9 skill files changed; `diff -r` with this branch's `system/.os/skills/` shows no difference |
| 4. Replace the app copy `.claude/skills/buildos-bulk-extract/` with the new folder | It holds `SKILL.md` only |
| 5. An npm install of `0.1.0` in the project (a second project): pin `0.2.0` | The wrapper skips the `0.1.0` install and asks `npx` for `0.2.0` (`notarget` before publication), so the step says to install `0.2.0` there too |
| 6. `.os/scripts/buildos version`, `help`, and the skill commands | `version: 0.2.0`; `help` lists `extract`, `fitgap`, and `export`; `export azure-boards adapters` exit 0; `extract bulk status` runs the command (exit 3 in this empty project, because it has no `.os/indexes/references.json` until intake builds it, as the skill says) |

### Owner Decision 2026-11-26 (F-P8-11)

The owner decided on 2026-11-26 (relayed by the orchestrating maintainer chat; recorded first in [Owner Decisions 2026-11-26 (Recorded in Review Round 1)](#owner-decisions-2026-11-26-recorded-in-review-round-1), item 1):

1. F-P8-11 is fixed in `0.2.0`. There is no `0.1.1`.
2. A command that BuildOS prints for the adopter to run takes the form `npx -y build-os@<running version> …`, which works on every system with no global install.

This is the owner decision that parity exception PE-023 needs. The Windows quoting (F-P8-10) is fixed in the same exception, under this decision: the printed command is new text in any case, and a quoting that the shell runs as shown is part of a command that runs as printed. Review round 1 narrowed "every system": the command is for POSIX `sh` on Linux and macOS and for Command Prompt on Windows (the Windows `action:` line now says so), and with the npm setting `bin-links=false` an `npx` run that caches the package without its link exits 127, and that cached copy keeps failing until it is removed (review round 2 narrowed this: a copy cached with its link runs); see [Review Round 1 (Pull Request 9)](#review-round-1-pull-request-9) and [Review Round 2 (Pull Request 9)](#review-round-2-pull-request-9).

### The Helper

`toolkits/buildos/src/core/shared/run-command.ts` builds every printed command (`runProgram`, `printedRun`, `runCommand`). Its rules, each with a test in `test/run-command.test.ts`:

| Input | Printed program | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A release version, `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` (`0.2.0`) | `npx -y build-os@0.2.0` | The printed command names the running program's version, and npm can hold that exact version. For a published release, that is the same package. A version stamp alone does not prove that the registry holds the same bytes: the end-to-end check below printed `@0.1.0` from a local build and ran the published `0.1.0`, a different build (review round 1). |
| A prerelease (`0.2.0-rc.1`) | `npx -y build-os@0.2.0-rc.1` | npm can hold an exact prerelease, and an exact pin installs it whatever its dist-tag. |
| A source build (`dev`), and the reserved `0.0.0-dev` | `buildos` | No npm version names this build, so an `npx` form cannot run it. `buildos` is the name a source build gets from `npm link` or a global install of its packed file. `buildos init` used this rule for its shown command since W1 R7 P6. |
| A version with build metadata (`0.2.0+local`), or any other text | `buildos` | npm drops `+local` and would run the registry `0.2.0`, a different build; the manifest contract does not accept such a version either. |

Quoting: a folder path (a `{ path }` word) is always quoted, as Go's `%q` always quoted the root, so the command has the same shape for every folder. POSIX gets single quotes (a `'` is written `'\''`), so the shell expands no `$`, backtick, or `\` in it; Go's `%q` double quotes did not stop `$` and backtick expansion. Windows gets Command Prompt double quotes (`quoteAlways` in `src/core/init/make-docs.ts`, the rule `buildos init` already used): each `\` is written once, a backslash run is doubled only before the closing quote, and a `%` is put outside the quotes as `^%`. Other words are quoted only when they hold a character outside the safe set.

### Parity Exception PE-023

`toolkits/buildos/test/golden/parity-exceptions.json`, PE-023, with the owner decision above. It is a class rule, like PE-016, held in its `printed_command` field: `applyPrintedCommands` in `test/golden/harness.ts` states the rule independently of the CLI code and turns each Go form into the port's form, in the text as printed and inside each JSON string (decoded, then encoded again with Go's escaping). Every other byte is compared as before.

| Form | Cases |
| --- | --- |
| `rebuild` (`buildos entities rebuild-index --root <Go %q root> --mode <mode> --apply`) | Goldens: 5 on darwin and linux (`entities-rebuild-check-stale-strict-json`, `entities-rebuild-apply-missing-json`, `entities-validate-missing-index-strict`, `entities-validate-missing-index-compat-json`, `entities-consolidate-apply-index-failure-json`) and 6 on win32 (the same 5 and `entities-rebuild-apply-write-failure-json`). Seeds: 11 entity edge seeds and 5 `$PWD` seeds. |
| `usage` (`Run buildos help for command syntax.`) | 7 shared goldens (`cli-version-bad-flag`, `cli-version-bad-flag-json`, `cli-version-help`, `cli-unknown-command`, `entities-validate-no-root-usage`, `entities-resolve-no-id-usage-json`, `entities-consolidate-extra-arg-usage`). For a development build this form is unchanged; it changes only in the release-identity comparison of the release gate. The P1 seed `cli-goldens.json` holds it 64 times; its test runs only a development build. |

Golden files changed: 0. `CAPTURE.md` says goldens never change; the approved mechanism is the exception, so the goldens stay the frozen Go baseline. `compare.test.ts` fails when a form occurs in a case that PE-023 does not list for the running system, or not in a listed one; `test/golden/printed-command.test.ts` checks that each list is exactly where each form occurs in the goldens of all three systems and in the seeds, that Go's own text, a bare `buildos` from a release build, and Go's `%q` root no longer match, and that no exact value pinned by another exception holds a Go-form command.

### Windows Quoting (F-P8-10)

Go's `%q` doubled each `\`. Command Prompt passes `"D:\\work\\root"` on unchanged, so the program got the doubled path; Windows path rules fold the doubled separators of a drive path, so the `0.1.0` command most likely ran there (not tested on Windows), but it showed the folder wrongly, and a UNC root (`\\server\share`) came out with four leading backslashes, which is not a UNC path. PE-023 prints `"D:\work\root"`, which both Command Prompt and PowerShell pass as one argument with single backslashes.

`test/run-command.test.ts` ("the printed rebuild command runs as printed in the system shell") takes the printed `action:` text of a source build, replaces only its program word `buildos` with `"<node>" "<bundle>"`, and runs it: in `sh` on Linux and macOS, for folders named `plain`, `with space`, and ``a$b `c` it's & (d)``; in Command Prompt (`cmd.exe /d /s /c`) and Windows PowerShell (`powershell.exe -Command "& …"`) on Windows, for `plain`, `with space`, and `a&b (c)`. Each run must exit 0 and write the index. Verified: macOS (`sh`, here); Linux and macOS (`sh`) and Windows Server 2025 (Command Prompt and Windows PowerShell) in CI; see [CI Run (F-P8-11)](#ci-run-f-p8-11). Not tested: a folder name with `$`, a backtick, or `%` in PowerShell (stated as a limit in `SECURITY.md`), PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`), and the `npx` program word on Windows (the published-smoke step 10 covers it on the next release).

### Published Smoke Step 10

`scripts/published-smoke.ts` gets step 10, last because it writes the project's entity index: `entities validate --json` in the project of step 3, then a check that `result.index.remediation_command` holds the rebuild command and that the human `action:` line of step 5 holds the same text. For `0.1.0` the step checks the bare `buildos` form (the known defect) and does not run it. For any later version the text must start with `npx -y build-os@<version> `, the step runs it as printed (`sh -c`, or Command Prompt on Windows), and `entities validate` must then print no index warning. Step counts: 13 on Linux and macOS (12 on Windows) for `0.1.0`, and 15 (14) for a later version; before this change they were 12 (11). A local run on macOS for `0.1.0`: "passed (13 of 13 steps)". The pull request runs the `buildos-smoke` workflow (its path filter names the script) for `0.1.0` on three systems.

## F-P9-04 Capability-Matrix Command (2026-11-26)

Branch `feat/capability-matrix-command`, stacked on pull request 9 (`fix/f-p8-11-printed-commands`, head `f93be66`), which was not merged when this work started. The owner decided on 2026-11-26 that the `capability-matrix` skill gets its own BuildOS command in `0.2.0`, so that no skill needs Python and the named exception of the no-Python check goes away (F-P9-04; see [Owner Decisions 2026-11-26 (Recorded in Review Round 1)](#owner-decisions-2026-11-26-recorded-in-review-round-1), item 2). This section records the design, written before the code, and then what was built. No version, release candidate, tag, release, or stage changed.

### The Tool (F-P9-04)

The skill `system/.os/skills/capability-matrix/SKILL.md` embeds its tool `cm_build.py` in the appendix "Appendix — `cm_build.py`" (a fenced `python` block, 271 lines) and tells the agent to write it to `build/cm_build.py` and run `python3 build/cm_build.py skeleton|assemble|fitgap|validate …`. The frozen source of behaviour is that block at commit `085927e3c1324fc73fe57af9493ca0b01fcaed18`, the first commit of the public repository and the revision the other three skill scripts are read from (`toolkits/buildos/test/golden/skills/script-source.ts`). `SKILL.md` is byte for byte the same at that commit, at `4dd86ce` (`main`), and at `f93be66`: SHA-256 `688b93048d50097644f72827f79a0e842bfcebca978e0c271c7b5b4a3b128a30`. The block (from the line after the opening fence to the line before the closing fence, with its final line break) has SHA-256 `559ccc27826acbb1dea53ebc829de0242922366672964beea218edd5f56d38a8`. It imports only the standard library (`argparse`, `csv`, `glob`, `json`, `os`, `re`, `sys`, `collections`).

| Subcommand | Options | Reads | Writes | Script exit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `skeleton` | `--skeleton` (required) | the skeleton JSON | nothing | 0; 1 with `FAIL` lines on stdout; 1 with a traceback |
| `assemble` | `--skeleton` (required), `--parts` (one or more, files or `glob` patterns), `--out` (required), `--date` (default empty) | the skeleton and each part (a JSON list of capabilities) | `<out>/<code>-capability-model.json` (`json.dump`, `indent=1`, `ensure_ascii=False`, no final line break), `<out>/<code>-capabilities.csv` and `<out>/<code>-requirements.csv` (`csv.writer`, UTF-8 with a byte order mark, `\r\n`); `<code>` is the system code in lower case | 0; 1 with `assemble: …` on stderr (`sys.exit`); 1 with a traceback |
| `fitgap` | `--mode` (`replacement`, the default, `selection`, or `integration`), `--baseline`, `--target`, `--models` (zero or more), `--rows` (one or more), `--only` (zero or more), `--out` (required), `--date` (default empty) | the models, the scored rows, the target-only rows | `<out>/<b>-<t>-fit-gap.csv` and `.json`, or in integration mode `<out>/<a>-<b>…-integration-map.csv` and `.json`; `<out>` is made first, before anything is read | 0; 1 with `fitgap: …` on stderr; 1 with a traceback |
| `validate` | `--model` (required), `--narrative`, `--fitgap`, `--baseline`, `--target` | the model, `<model folder>/<code>-capabilities.csv` and `-requirements.csv`, the narrative, the fit/gap and its two models | nothing | 0 with `ALL CHECKS PASSED`; 1 with `*** N FAILURE(S) ***`; 1 with a traceback |

argparse prints its usage and exits 2 for a missing required option, an unknown option, a value not in `--mode`'s choices, or no subcommand.

### Design (Before the Code)

Name and shape: `buildos capability-matrix skeleton|assemble|fitgap|validate`, with the script's options and the shared `--root`, `--json`, `--allow-outside-root`, and `--help`. The domain is named after the skill, as `buildos fitgap` is named after the tool of `fit-gap-analysis` and `buildos export azure-boards` after its target. The script's own name (`cm_build`) says nothing to an adopter, and its `fitgap` subcommand cannot be a domain, because `buildos fitgap` is the fit-gap-analysis command; under `capability-matrix` it is a subcommand and does not clash. PRD 20 Command Surface lists each `0.2.0` command in its table; this one is added there. Usage and help name `buildos` (PRD 20 Output and Exit Contract, SD-02).

Built by the method of P9 Stages 1 and 2:

- Core logic in `toolkits/buildos/src/core/capability-matrix/`, on the shared Python ports (`py-json.ts` for `json.load` and `json.dump`, `fitgap/py.ts` for Python value rules, the `glob` and `fnmatch` port of `buildos fitgap`, the `csv` reader of `extract/py-lines.ts`). The CLI adapter is `src/cli/commands/capability-matrix.ts`; it owns the parse, the output, and the exit code. Every write goes through the write plan of `ProjectFiles` (the filesystem port).
- Writes follow the tool they replace: the script writes when it runs, with no dry run, so the command does too, as `buildos fitgap` does (no `--apply`).
- Human stdout and stderr are the script's, byte for byte. `--json` prints the shared envelope with `result.output` (the stdout lines) and `result.written`, as `buildos fitgap` does.
- Exit codes map as SD-01 maps `fitgap.py`: 0 done; 2 usage; 3 a file that cannot be read or has the wrong shape (the script's traceback); 4 a stop (`sys.exit` with a message) or a failed check (`FAIL` lines); 5 a failed write; 10 a write whose undo was incomplete.
- Goldens: invented fixtures under `test/fixtures/skills/capability-matrix/` (the one neutral topic of the skill fixtures, a community library), captured by running the pinned block with Python 3 through `test/golden/skills/capture.ts`, which gains a fourth script without changing the other three's goldens. The parity test compares every golden byte for byte.

Intended divergences, each forced by a rule the owner already decided (none needs an owner decision, except the one in the last row):

| SD | Divergence | Rule that forces it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SD-01 (rows added) | Exit codes as above; the script exits 1 for every failure and 2 for argparse | PRD 20 Output and Exit Contract |
| SD-02 (steps added) | Usage errors and help name `buildos`; no argparse abbreviations | PRD 20 Output and Exit Contract |
| SD-23 (new) | A traceback becomes one plain line on stderr, `capability-matrix <subcommand>: <what>`, exit 3; stdout up to that point stays the script's | PRD 20 (no stack trace), as SD-03 and SD-11 |
| SD-24 (new) | Contained, checked, atomic reads and writes, as SD-04, SD-05, SD-06, and SD-13 already hold for `buildos fitgap`: every file read and every pattern match is inside the project folder; every output is inside it unless `--allow-outside-root` is given; the out folder is made only when the run writes, and a failed run writes nothing (the script made `--out` before any check, and left a partial file when it crashed after its first write); a companion CSV path that falls outside the project (`validate --model model.json` with no folder: the script looked for `/<code>-capabilities.csv`) counts as missing | PRD 20 Output and Exit Contract; SD-04 (owner decision 2026-11-25) |
| SD-07 (applies) | Printed paths are as given; the root is never resolved through links | PRD 20 (one root model) |
| SD-25 (new) | Written files and printed text are the same bytes on every system: Python's text mode wrote `\r\n` for each `\n` of the model JSON and of stdout on Windows | PRD 20 Compatibility (the same input gives the same bytes) |
| SD-26 (new, owner question) | The script puts the system code into a regular expression unescaped (`re.fullmatch(rf'{code}-[A-Z]{{2,4}}-\d{{2,3}}[a-z]?', id)`). For a code with a pattern character (`\ . ^ $ * + ? { } [ ] | ( )`), Python's result depends on Python's pattern syntax (a code `A(` crashes, a code `A.B` also accepts `AxB-…`). BuildOS stops with a plain message (exit 4) instead of guessing Python's pattern rules | Owner question Q1 below; decided by the owner on 2026-11-27, option A |

Owner question Q1 (SD-26): (A) keep the stop for a code with a pattern character (recommended: real codes are letters and digits, the skill asks for a short upper-case code, and a stop names the code to change); (B) read the code as plain text in the id check, which differs from the script only for such codes. Decided by the owner on 2026-11-27, option A: "Yes, agreed: Stop with a clear message." ([Owner Decisions of 2026-11-27](#owner-decisions-of-2026-11-27-020-release)).

### Fixtures and Goldens (F-P9-04)

Captured on 2026-11-27 (the record's `provenance.captures` date; the work day is 2026-11-26 in the records) with Python 3.14.10, Node 26.13.1, macOS arm64, from the block pinned above, run as `python3 -P -s cm_build.py …` in a fresh copy of the base project per case. The tool reads no clock. 15 cases, 66 steps:

| Subcommand | Steps | Exit 0 | Exit 1 (a stop, FAIL lines, or a crash) | Exit 2 (argparse) | What they reach |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `skeleton` | 12 | 2 | 8 | 2 | a valid skeleton with a child capability; a converted one with thin scope briefs; every check that fails; layer columns from ids, codes, and names that are numbers, `null`, or `true` (Python's `1` and `True` are one key); a missing file, broken JSON, a byte order mark, a missing key, an id with no dash, a `null` layer id |
| `assemble` | 20 | 10 | 9 | 1 | restored fields, renumbered requirements, stripped and aliased option fields (every alias), pipe normalisation, CSV quoting (comma, quote, line break), non-ASCII text, `1.0`, `1e16`, an integer above 2^53, strings and dicts where lists belong, `null` and number summaries, a system key named `generated`; a pattern of parts; the same part twice; missing and extra capabilities; a pattern that matches nothing; statuses outside the vocabulary; a part that is not JSON; a missing key |
| `fitgap` | 13 | 3 | 9 | 1 | replacement with a pattern and target-only rows; selection; integration with two models; an unknown baseline id; an unknown target id; target ids as a string (read by character); an unknown target-only id; no `--baseline`; no `--models`; an empty `--models`; rows that are not JSON; a missing model |
| `validate` | 18 | 5 | 12 | 1 | a model with a narrative (CRLF, `§`, a bold status tag on the next line, trailing spaces); without one; with each fit/gap mode passing and failing; a wrong narrative; a model that fails every check; no companion CSVs; CSVs with CRLF, a quoted line break, a blank line, and padded counts; a count that is not a number; an unresolved parent; a missing narrative; a fit/gap without its models; a model that is not JSON |
| no subcommand, an unknown one, `--help` | 3 | 1 | 0 | 2 | argparse errors and help |

Not covered by goldens, and why: a run that crashed after its first write (the script left a partial file; the parity test compares written files strictly), a lone surrogate, a code with a pattern character, and a read or write outside the project. Each is a divergence held by `test/capability-matrix.test.ts` instead. A folder where a file belongs (`IsADirectoryError`) is a unit test too, so the Windows CI job does not depend on how a directory read fails there. Python's own regular-expression and Unicode tables are those of Python 3.14.10 (`unicodedata` 16.0.0); BuildOS uses Node's tables (Node 26.13.1: Unicode 17.0, ICU 78.3) for `\d` (also in argparse's negative-number check, review round 3 of pull request 10, finding 3), for lower case, and for which characters `repr` prints or escapes, which can differ only for characters that Unicode 17.0 added. Example (review round 2, finding 4): a missing id that is the one character U+11DE1 is `['\U00011de1']` in Python's message and `['𑷡']` in BuildOS's, because U+11DE1 is unassigned (not printable) in Unicode 16.0; `test/capability-matrix.test.ts` pins it. No table of Python's printable set is in the repository, and `py-json.ts` is shared, so the other commands keep Node's tables too.

### Divergences (F-P9-04)

Every divergence is in `test/golden/skills/divergences.json`. SD-01, SD-02, SD-07, and SD-23 to SD-25 follow rules that the owner already decided (PRD 20 exit codes, help and usage, no stack trace, one root model, SD-04 contained reads, SD-05 atomic writes, the same bytes on every system). SD-26 was not decided when it was built: owner question Q1 above. Decided by the owner on 2026-11-27, option A.

| SD | What differs from `cm_build.py` |
| --- | --- |
| SD-01 | Exit 2 for argparse usage, 3 for a crash (a traceback), 4 for a stop or FAIL lines, 5 for a failed write, 10 for an incomplete undo; the script exited 1 or 2 |
| SD-02 | Usage errors and help name `buildos`; no argparse abbreviations (`--skel`) |
| SD-23 | A crash is one plain line, `capability-matrix <subcommand>: <what>`, exit 3; stdout up to there is the script's |

#### JavaScript and Python Numbers (Audit)

Checked in `cm-build.ts` and `py-values.ts`, each against Python's rule:

- Equality (`==`, `!=`): the restored fields (`layer_id`, `doc_ref`, `type`, `name`), `r['id'] != rid`, the id prefix against the layer code, `kind == 'setting'`, a child's `doc_ref` against its parent's, a heading against a name, the fit/gap mode. Exact for integers above 2^53, `1 == 1.0 == True`, `-0.0 == 0`, `2**53 + 1 != 2.0**53`, `0.5 != 0`, `'1' != 1`; a NaN is unequal to itself.
- Identity first (`PyObject_RichCompareBool`): the items of a list or a dict in `==`, `x in list`, a tuple of verdicts, and `list.index` (the sort keys of `assemble` and `fitgap`). Every NaN that `json` reads is the one object `json.decoder.NaN`, so a NaN equals a NaN there.
- Dictionary keys and set members: `LC`, `LM`, `skel`, `PM`, `IDX`, the per-row `ids`, the narrative `heads`, the id sets of `skeleton`, `assemble`, and `validate`, the target statuses and maturities, and every `Counter`. Integer precision kept; `1`, `1.0`, and `True` one key (the first key kept, the last value); `'1'` and `1` two keys; every NaN one key; an unhashable key names its use in Python 3.14's words (`cannot use 'list' as a set element (unhashable type: 'list')`, `as a dict key`; plain `unhashable type: 'list'` for `Counter(...)`).
- Sorting: `sorted(miss)`, `sorted(extra)`, the sorted target statuses and maturities, and the vocabularies. Numbers by exact value (`1.5 < 2**53 < 2**53 + 1`, `inf` above any integer), strings by code point, `None < None` a `TypeError`. A set that mixes unorderable values, or holds a NaN, is sorted from its first-seen order: new divergence SD-27, because Python's own order there changes with the hash seed (checked with `PYTHONHASHSEED` 0 to 5 and random).
- Arithmetic: requirement counts and lengths are small JavaScript integers; the CSV count column is summed as `bigint` and compared with `BigInt(len(reqs))`.
- Text of a number: `str`, `repr`, f-strings, `csv` fields, and `json.dump` keep every digit of an integer and write a float as `repr` (`1.0`, `-0.0`, `1e+16`, `inf` in text, `Infinity` and `NaN` in JSON), and a `Counter` key as `json` writes it (`"true"`, `"1.0"`, `"9007199254740993"`).
- Reading: an integer is a `number` when safe, else a `bigint`; the 4,300-digit limit of `int()` for JSON and for the CSV count.
- Not reached: an integer used as a list index (every index in the tool is a constant).

Seen while auditing, outside this command: `fitgap/py.ts` (`pyEq`, `hashKey`, `pyCompare`) still turns a `bigint` into a JavaScript number for `buildos fitgap`, and `buildos fitgap` reads an empty pattern as the project folder where `fitgap.py` found no file (`glob.glob('')` and `os.path.exists('')`). Neither was changed here: follow-up F-P9-12.

Root safety record (SD-24): the reviewer found no outside content read, no listing, no unauthorized write, and no existing-versus-missing disclosure, but a valid absolute input caused metadata lookups (stat) of eight paths outside the declared root without the switch. They come from the identity check of P9-R2-10 (`insideByIdentity` in `project-files.ts`): to recognize the project folder under another spelling, BuildOS looks at the device and inode of the typed path and of each of its parent folders, from the path upward, and the one-name-at-a-time lookup does this for each folder of the path. SD-24 said such folders are never looked at; that was false. SD-24, `SECURITY.md` (Paths Outside the Project), and the `osLookup` comment now say exactly what is looked at (metadata of the path's folders, to recognize the root under another spelling; never content, never a listing) and why. The lookup code is unchanged in this pass.

A test splits that line by the Command Prompt rules (no `& | < > ^ ( )` outside quotes, no `%` or `!`; then the Microsoft C runtime rules that Node.js uses for its arguments), checks that it gives the same words as the `sh` example and the JSON `{"publisher_prefix":"ex_"}`, and runs those words on an emitted CSV (exit 0). The wrapper `buildos.cmd` passes `%*` on unchanged. It was not run in Command Prompt on Windows; the Windows CI job runs the test, which reads the line, not Command Prompt. `ADAPTER.md` already differed from `v0.1.0`, so guide chapter 4's upgrade table still lists exactly the files that differ (15 files, checked with `git diff --stat v0.1.0 -- system/`).

## Version 0.2.0 and the Release Runbook (2026-11-27)

W1 R7 P9 t13, first part, on the branch `release/0.2.0-version`. It sets the version to `0.2.0`, puts the `0.2.0` release notes in their final form, lists every open follow-up with its place before or after the release, and writes the release runbook. It follows the pattern of the `0.1.0` version change (`df3ff9b`, pull request 1: the version in `package.json` and `package-lock.json`, the evidence, and a history record). Nothing is published: no dry-run branch, tag, release, stage, `buildos-release` run, merge, or settings change, and `release-candidates.json` is unchanged (the `0.1.0` entry stays; the `0.2.0` entry comes from the dry-run tarball, step d below). The branch is stacked on pull request 10 (`feat/capability-matrix-command`, head `5f87063`), which is stacked on pull request 9 (`fix/f-p8-11-printed-commands`, head `f93be66`); neither is merged into `main` (`4dd86ce`) on 2026-11-27.

After publication it moves to `0.2.0` with its test (`test/release-workflow.test.ts`, "default 0.1.0"), step k below.

### A Staged Version Cannot Be Installed Before Approval

npm's documentation: `npm stage publish` "places that version of the package into the registry in a state where it's not available for public access" (`npm help stage`, npm 11.20.0), and "the staged version and its contents are not publicly available until a maintainer approves the staged package" (docs.npmjs.com, Staged publishing, read on 2026-11-27). npm documents `npm stage download <stage-id>` "for inspection" (no 2FA; the package's writer only) and documents no install of a staged version. `SECURITY.md` already says: "A staged package is not public." The `0.1.0` records hold no install of a staged version: the owner approved the stage before the Stage 4 checks, and they ran on the published package under the owner decision of 2026-11-26 ([Post-Publication Checks of 0.1.0](#post-publication-checks-of-010-2026-11-26)).

So the `buildos-smoke` workflow and `npx -y build-os@0.2.0` cannot reach a staged, unapproved `0.2.0`: both read the public registry. Before approval, the smoke runs on the release tarball instead. It has the same bytes as the staged package: the `stage` job stages exactly the release asset, after it checks the asset against the reviewed entry and the release run's own rebuild ([Release Procedure](../../../toolkits/buildos/SECURITY.md#release-procedure)), and the maintainer can prove it for the stage with `npm stage download <stage-id>` and a SHA-256 (step h1). The dry-run artifact's tarball is the same file again: the reviewed entry is computed from it (step d). So the tarball smoke can run as early as step c, before anything is fixed, and this runbook recommends that.

`scripts/published-smoke.ts` has no tarball input: every step runs `npx -y build-os@<version>` against the registry, and the project wrapper falls back to the same fetch. A tarball input changes each `npx` step (`npx -y --package <tarball> -- buildos …`), adds a local install so the wrapper steps run the pinned version without the registry, makes step 10 run the printed `npx -y build-os@<version>` command against that local install, and needs a workflow input that downloads and checks the file. That is more than a few lines, so it is not built here. Built on 2026-11-27 in pull request 12 ([F-P9-15 Smoke on a Release Tarball](#f-p9-15-smoke-on-a-release-tarball-2026-11-27)). New follow-up F-P9-15: give `scripts/published-smoke.ts` a `--tarball <file> --sha256 <hex>` input (the same 13 or 15 steps on the local file, with no registry fetch of `build-os`) and `.github/workflows/buildos-smoke.yml` an input that downloads the tarball of a named `buildos-release` dry run (`actions: read`, no secret) and checks its SHA-256 before the steps, with tests in `test/release-workflow.test.ts` and `test/post-publication-scripts.test.ts`. It must merge before the commit that the dry run builds (step a), because the tag commit may differ from the reviewed commit only in the ledger. The orchestrator decided on 2026-11-27 to build it (below; the owner may overrule).

`PERF-002` measures `npx -y build-os@<version> version` with an empty npm cache against the registry, and its instrument fetches `https://registry.npmjs.org/build-os/-/build-os-<version>.tgz` (`scripts/measure-npx-first-run.ts`). It cannot run on a staged version either. The `PERF-002` profile expires "at the next release that changes the package size", and its requalification authority is "the work phase of that release", which is P9; P9's testing decisions have Performance Testing `not-needed-now`. Before approval, the tarball size against `0.1.0` (1,070,295 bytes, 173 files) is known from step c, and no `0.2.0` performance measurement exists. The orchestrator decided on 2026-11-27 on one pass after publication (below; the owner may overrule).

### Trusted Publishing and Settings Before the Release

The trusted publisher for `build-os` exists (First Publication steps 4 and 5, 2026-11-26, owner-reported), and the first publish through it succeeded (`build-os@0.1.0`, release run 45894295344). npm's documentation (docs.npmjs.com, Trusted publishers, read on 2026-11-27): "A newly created trusted publisher configuration must complete its first successful publish within 2 days", and the first successful publish "validates the configuration and binds it to the repository's immutable identity". It names no expiry after that. So nothing in the trust setup expires before `0.2.0`. Its fields must match exactly ("All fields are case-sensitive and must be exact"): this branch keeps the workflow file `.github/workflows/buildos-release.yml` and the environment `buildos-npm-stage` (checked: the `stage` job's `environment: buildos-npm-stage`). Before step f, the owner reads the configuration (an agent never runs `npm trust`): `npm trust list build-os` must show GitHub Actions, `brucewaynedecoy/build-os`, `buildos-release.yml`, `buildos-npm-stage`, staged publishing only. The owner's npm account needs two-factor authentication for the stage approval. The `deny-list` and `stage` jobs of each prepare and release run check again that the rulesets are active with the needed rules and that the environments limit their refs. They cannot check two settings: who may bypass a ruleset (GitHub returns the bypass list only to a user with write access to the ruleset, which the job token is not) and the repository setting for release immutability (it needs the Administration permission). `scripts/release-github.ts` prints this limit in its `rulesets` result. The `stage` job checks only that the published release is immutable. So the owner checks both settings at step f, before publishing the draft. The dry-run artifact is kept 3 days, so steps b to d, h2, and h3 fit in 3 days.

### Who Starts the Dry Run (the 0.1.0 Records)

`SECURITY.md` and `toolkits/buildos/AGENTS.md` say "No agent publishes, stages, tags, creates a release, runs `npm trust`, or changes repository or npm settings". They do not name the dry run, and the trust rule lets anyone with write access push a branch. A dry run holds no secret and stages nothing (`resolve` and `verify` only). The records: the `0.1.0` dry run [45888733182](https://github.com/brucewaynedecoy/build-os/actions/runs/45888733182) was a `workflow_dispatch` from `main` on `20f941a` (purpose `dry-run`, candidates `self`), and GitHub names `brucewaynedecoy` as its actor and triggering actor (`gh api repos/brucewaynedecoy/build-os/actions/runs/45888733182`, read on 2026-11-27); no record says whether the owner or the orchestrator started it, and an agent here uses the owner's `gh` login, so GitHub's actor cannot tell them apart. In the earlier repository, the dry runs on `release-dry-run/980b67a` and the planted-failure branches were pushed and reported by the orchestrator ([P8 CI Runs and Dry Run on 980b67a](#p8-ci-runs-and-dry-run-on-980b67a)), and the branch was deleted after its run. Following those records, an agent may start the `0.2.0` dry run when the owner says go, and records who started it. The owner then accepts the tarball (step d).

### Release Runbook for 0.2.0

Every step names who does it. "Agent" steps need the owner's go. No agent publishes, stages, tags, creates or publishes a release, approves a deployment or a stage, runs `npm trust`, records an owner decision that the owner has not made, or changes a setting. Do the steps in this order; the order that was missed for `0.1.0` (the npm approval before the checks) is prevented here by the owner, not by a tool: step j has three preconditions that the owner checks at that step. Nothing technical stops an early approval. After step g, a maintainer can approve the stage with 2FA at once, in the CLI or on npmjs.com, and npm does not look at h1 to h5 or at step i. The workflow only stages and prints instructions. npm's documentation describes an explicit approval, and gives no auto-approval and no expiry date for a stage. So step j is an owner-enforced gate. In commands, `<M>` is the full SHA of the `main` commit that the dry run builds (the merge commit of this pull request, or a later `main` commit, step 0), `<short>` its first 7 characters, `<run>` a run ID, `<attempt>` its run attempt, and `$D` a new empty folder outside the repository (`D=$(mktemp -d)`). Each command says where it runs: "the repository root" or `toolkits/buildos/` of a clean checkout of `<M>`, or "any folder" when it reads only `$D` and the network.


The three jobs `smoke (tarball, <os>, Node 24)` pass: 20 of 20 steps on Linux and macOS, 19 of 19 on Windows. In each downloaded `smoke-<os>.json`, `passed` is `true`, `mode` is `tarball`, `tarball.sha256` is `<sha256>`, `tarball.version` is `0.2.0`, `tarball_mode.proves` holds four claims (the registry guard, the direct steps, the wrapper, and step 10's run of the printed command), `tarball_mode.not_proven` and `tarball_mode.not_run` are empty, and `absolute_paths_removed` is `0`. `launchers` records the launchers and the entry scripts that the launch probe observed (review round 2 of pull request 12, finding 1; review round 3, findings 1 and 2): `launchers.npm_programs` lists the selected npm's program files below `{NPM}`; on Linux and macOS each launcher of `launchers.npx` resolves into `{TMP}/npm-cache/_npx/<hash>/node_modules/build-os/` and each of `launchers.project` into `{TMP}/project/node_modules/build-os/`, and on Windows each shim of both is "byte-equal to the canonical shim of the selected npm's cmd-shim"; `launchers.wrapper_lookup` is `{TMP}/project/node_modules/build-os/dist/buildos.js`; and each entry of `launchers.observed` lists only programs of `launchers.npm_programs`, the project's `.os/scripts/pinned-version.cjs` (step 9), and the expected bin file of those copies. This is what the probe observed: a process that is not Node.js, or a Node.js process started with a cleared environment, is not observed (`launchers.observes`). Start this run on its own and read it on its own (`gh run view <smoke-run>` of this run ID, not the newest run of the list): a hand-started run has its own concurrency group, so it is never cancelled by another hand-started run (review round 3 of pull request 12, finding 6).    ```sh


     ```sh

     curl -sS -X POST https://rekor.sigstore.dev/api/v1/index/retrieve -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"hash\":\"sha512:$H\"}"
     curl -sS https://rekor.sigstore.dev/api/v1/log/entries/<uuid>
     ```

     The first `curl` prints the UUIDs of the log entries for that hash. One of them must be the entry that the `stage` job's log names (the job prints `https://search.sigstore.dev/?logIndex=<index>`; the second `curl` prints the `logIndex` of a UUID). ### Orchestrator Decisions (2026-11-27)

The owner's orchestrator decided these on 2026-11-27, after review round 1 of pull request 11. They are orchestrator decisions, not owner decisions; the owner may overrule each one.

## F-P9-15 Smoke on a Release Tarball (2026-11-27)

Follow-up F-P9-15, built on branch `feat/smoke-a-tarball` (pull request 12, stacked on pull requests 11, 10, and 9), under the orchestrator decision of 2026-11-27 ([Orchestrator Decisions (2026-11-27)](#orchestrator-decisions-2026-11-27)). `build-os@0.1.0` was approved on npm before its smoke ran, because the smoke could test only a published version, and a staged version cannot be installed before approval ([A Staged Version Cannot Be Installed Before Approval](#a-staged-version-cannot-be-installed-before-approval)). So `scripts/published-smoke.ts` and `.github/workflows/buildos-smoke.yml` now also run on a release tarball, which has the same bytes as the stage. No product code (`src/`), version, `release-candidates.json`, or `buildos-release.yml` changed. The package file list is unchanged (168 files; the scripts do not ship).

### How Each Step Gets the Package (F-P9-15)

The script takes `--tarball <file> --sha256 <hex>` in place of `--version <version>` (the two are exclusive). The file's SHA-256 must equal `--sha256` before any step runs, and the version is read from `package/package.json` in the tarball (name `build-os`, a plain version). The new module `scripts/smoke-source.ts` holds the mode switch, the tarball identity, the registry guard, and the limits, with no process start, so the tests run it with stubs. Each step stays as close as possible to what an adopter runs:

| Step | Registry mode | Tarball mode | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 to 7 and the `entities validate --json` runs of step 10 | `npx -y build-os@<version> <command>` | `npx -y --package=<tarball> -- buildos <command>` (step 7: `npx -y --package=<tarball> buildos-intake --help`) | npx installs the file into its own cache folder and starts the bin, as it does for a registry version; only the package spec differs. |
| 8, the wrapper with Node.js missing | No package | No package | Unchanged. |
| New, before step 9 | None | `npm install --offline --ignore-scripts --no-save --no-package-lock --prefix <project> <tarball>` | The offline install of the user guide (chapter 4). The wrapper accepts a local install only when its version equals the pin (pin first, `SECURITY.md` "Rollback by Version Pin"); `init` from the tarball pinned `0.2.0`, which is not on the registry, so without it the wrapper's `npx` fallback could not run. |
| 9, the wrapper with Node.js present | The wrapper's `npx -y build-os@<pin>` fallback | The wrapper runs the pinned version from the project's local install | The documented local-install route of the wrapper. |
| 10, the printed fix command | Checks the printed text exactly, then runs it through `sh -c` (Command Prompt with delayed expansion off on Windows) | The same exact checks of the JSON field and the human `action:` line, then the same text through the same shell; npm resolves `build-os@0.2.0` to the project's local install of the tarball (npm takes an installed package of exactly the named version from the local tree) | The printed program, arguments, and quoting run as printed, on the tarball's bytes. The step name records that the registry fetch of the literal command is proven only after publication (runbook step k). |

What tarball mode proves in a run is made from the steps that ran and their outcomes (review round 1 of pull request 12, finding 2; [Review Round 1 (Pull Request 12)](#review-round-1-pull-request-12-2026-11-27)): when every step passes, every step ran the bytes of the tarball whose SHA-256 the report records, the direct steps ran through npx, the wrapper ran the pinned version from a local install of the tarball, and step 10's printed text is exact and works when run as printed. What it does not prove in any run: that `npx -y build-os@<version>` fetches the package from the registry (the literal printed command with a registry fetch, and the wrapper's `npx` fallback; runbook step k), and that the registry copy has the same bytes (runbook steps h1 and k). The report (`smoke-<os>.json`) records `mode`, `package_source`, `tarball` (file name, SHA-256, integrity, name, version, file count, and the SHA-256 of each bin file), and `tarball_mode` with `proves`, `not_proven`, `not_run`, and `does_not_prove`; `smoke-<os>.md` repeats them.

### The Registry Guard (F-P9-15)

Every process that the smoke starts in tarball mode gets `npm_config_offline=true` and `npm_config_registry=http://127.0.0.1:9/` (a closed local port), after the caller's own offline, prefer-online, prefer-offline, and registry settings are dropped in any spelling. npm then makes no network request, and a request for `build-os` from a registry fails with `ENOTCACHED` (a test runs this with real npm). After review round 1 of pull request 12 (finding 1), the guard also sets the new npm cache and a new empty global prefix in one spelling only, and requires positive evidence for each copy that ran: a preflight before step 1 (when it fails, the run stops and runs no other step), a check of the npx install after step 7, a check of the project install (and the npx install again) after step 10, and a check of the npm cache last ([Review Round 1 (Pull Request 12)](#review-round-1-pull-request-12-2026-11-27)). So tarball mode has 20 steps on Linux and macOS and 19 on Windows (15 and 14, plus the preflight, the two install checks, the install, and the cache check). Before that round, it had 18 and 17 (one last guard step).

### The Workflow (F-P9-15)

`workflow_dispatch` takes `source` (`registry`, `release-run`, or `release-tag`), `version` (registry, default `0.1.0`), `release_run` and `release_run_attempt` (release-run), `release_tag` (release-tag), and `tarball_sha256` (both tarball sources, required). The `check the inputs` job checks every value before any other job uses it (a version is a plain semver version, a run ID and attempt are digits only, a tag is `v` and a plain version of at most 128 characters, a SHA-256 is 64 lowercase hex characters, and the inputs of the other sources are empty), and later jobs get only the checked values, through `env:`. Runbook step c uses `release-run` (the dry-run artifact, kept 3 days); step h2 uses `release-tag` (the asset of the published GitHub Release `v0.2.0`, public and immutable).

| Job | Permissions | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `check-inputs` | `contents: read` (workflow) | Checks the inputs; no checkout. |
| `fetch-run` (release-run) | `contents: read`, `actions: read`; the job token as `GH_TOKEN` | Checks that the run's workflow is `.github/workflows/buildos-release.yml`, logs its event, head, status, and conclusion, downloads `buildos-release-<run>-<attempt>` with `gh run download`, requires exactly one `build-os-<version>.tgz` (a regular file) with the given SHA-256, and keeps it as the artifact `buildos-smoke-input-<run id>-<attempt>` (3 days). It runs no repository code. |
| `fetch-tag` (release-tag) | `contents: read` | Downloads `https://github.com/<repository>/releases/download/<tag>/build-os-<version>.tgz` with `curl` over `https` only (at most 64 MiB, no token; a draft release has no public URL), requires the given SHA-256, and keeps it the same way. |
| `smoke` (macOS, Linux, Windows; Node 24) | `contents: read` | Registry mode: the script with `--version`. Tarball mode: downloads the checked file from this run, by the artifact ID that the fetch job's upload returned (a job output; review round 1 of pull request 12, finding 4), and runs the script with `--tarball` and the given `--sha256`. Local-pack (pull request): `check-dependencies`, `npm ci --ignore-scripts`, `check-dependencies --installed`, `scripts/release-build.ts`, then the script on that tarball with its SHA-256. The output is kept as `buildos-smoke-<mode>-<os>` (30 days). |

The workflow keeps the smoke rules: `contents: read` at the top, no secret, no environment, no OIDC token, actions pinned by SHA, `persist-credentials: false`, npm install scripts off, no `${{ }}` in a `run:` script, and no `pull_request_target`. A pull request that changes the workflow or the smoke scripts (`published-smoke.ts`, `printed-fix-step.ts`, `smoke-evidence.ts`, `smoke-source.ts`, `tar-reader.mjs`) runs the registry mode on `0.1.0` and the tarball mode on a release build of its own tree on the three systems, so the tarball mode is tested in CI before a release needs it.

### How the Guard Proves Which Bytes Ran (Pull Request 12)

What npm records was read in the npm of CI, npm 11.19.1 (pacote 21.5.1, cacache 20.0.4, libnpmexec 10.3.2, whose code is the same as in npm 11.20.0 used locally), and checked with real runs. Every process gets `npm_config_offline=true`, the blocked registry, the run's new npm cache, and a new empty global prefix below the run's root, each in one spelling (the caller's value of each, in any case or `-`/`_` spelling, is dropped). The temporary root is used by its real path: through a linked path (macOS `/var` and `/tmp`), npm writes the hidden lockfile keys relative to the link.

- Steps 1 to 7 (the npx copy). `npx --package=<file>` installs a spec that is not in the local tree into `<cache>/_npx/<hash>`, writes the spec to that folder's `package.json` (`_npx.packages`), and starts the bin with that folder's `node_modules/.bin` first on `PATH`, before each `node_modules/.bin` from the working folder up and the caller's `PATH` (`@npmcli/run-script` `set-path.js`). It does not look at a global install when `--package` is given. After step 7, before the project install exists, the check needs: exactly one npx folder, whose `_npx.packages` is exactly the tarball file; its `node_modules/build-os` holds exactly the tarball's files (each by its path, with the tarball's SHA-256, and no other file); its hidden lockfile entry has the tarball's version, a `file:` spec with the tarball's name, and the tarball's integrity; and no other `node_modules/build-os` folder below the run's root (the global prefix is there too).
- Steps 9 and 10 (the project copy). After step 10, the project's `node_modules/build-os` passes the same file and lockfile checks, the npx install passes its checks again (the `entities validate --json` runs of step 10 used it), and no other `build-os` folder is below the root.
- Every read of the tarball (the npm cache). The cache index (`<cache>/_cacache/index-v5`, one `<hash>\t<JSON>` line per entry) must hold at least one entry, and each entry must have the key `pacote:tarball:file:<path>` with the tarball's file name and the integrity `sha512-<base64 SHA-512 of the file>`, which the script computes from the file. The cache content for that integrity (`content-v2/sha512/<2>/<2>/<rest of the hex digest>`) must have the tarball's SHA-256. An empty index, a registry response, or an entry for another file fails.

So tarball mode has 20 steps on Linux and macOS and 19 on Windows for `0.2.0`, and 18 and 17 for a `0.1.0` tarball (whose step 10 checks the bare form and runs nothing).

The two hand-started `0.1.0` runs of [CI Run (F-P9-15)](#ci-run-f-p9-15) (45980577022 and 45980854201) wrote reports whose `tarball_mode.proves` held the fixed sentence that step 10 ran the printed fix through a shell, while their step 10 ran nothing (finding 2). Their step results stand; that sentence of their reports is wrong, and reports made after this fix do not have it.

### Launchers and Launch Records (Pull Request 12)

Corrected in review round 3 of pull request 12 (2026-11-27, findings 1 and 2; [Review Round 3 and the Final Fix Pass](#review-round-3-and-the-final-fix-pass-pull-request-12-2026-11-27)): this section first claimed that a run proves which executable each step ran, and the Windows shims were read by parsing their target. The claim is now limited to the entry scripts of the Node.js processes that the launch probe observed, the npm programs are the exact files of the one selected npm installation, and each Windows shim must be byte-equal to the canonical shim. The text below says what round 2 built.

Two independent records, per route, on each system. Neither changes product code.

- The launchers (static). npx starts a bin by name from its folder's `node_modules/.bin`, and a shell starts the printed `npx -y build-os@<version>` command, whose package npm finds in the project and whose bin `build-os` it starts from the project's `node_modules/.bin`. So each launcher must resolve to the bin's file inside the verified copy: the npx route `buildos` and `buildos-intake` (steps 1 to 7 and the `entities validate --json` runs of step 10) into `<cache>/_npx/<hash>/node_modules/build-os/dist/`, and the project route `build-os` and `buildos` into `<project>/node_modules/build-os/dist/`. On macOS and Linux npm makes a symbolic link, and the check reads its real path (a regular file there is not npm's launcher and fails). On Windows npm makes a `.cmd` shim (what Command Prompt and npm's run-script start) and a PowerShell shim (cmd-shim 8 in npm 11); the check reads the one target that each names (`"%dp0%\<path>"`, `"$basedir/<path>"`, the shim's own `node.exe` aside), resolves it against the shim's folder, and compares it case-insensitively. The project wrapper does not use a launcher: its helper's `localEntry` (the first lookup that `pinned-version.cjs` makes, in the project folder) must choose the project install's `buildos` bin file; the check calls that exported function with `node -e`, which starts no BuildOS.
- The run itself (dynamic). Every Node.js process of a tarball-mode step loads a launch probe first (`NODE_OPTIONS=--require "<probe>"`; the caller's `NODE_OPTIONS` is replaced in tarball mode), which appends `process.argv[1]` and its real path (the file that Node.js loads as the main script) to the step's own launch log and prints nothing. Apart from npm's own programs (`npm-cli.js`, `npx-cli.js`, and on Windows `npm-prefix.js`, which npm's `npx.cmd` shim starts first, in the `bin` folder of an npm install) and, for step 9, the wrapper's helper, every recorded program must be the expected bin file of the verified copy, and at least one must be: `dist/buildos.js` of the npx copy for steps 1 to 6 and the validate runs of step 10, `dist/buildos-intake.js` of the npx copy for the legacy name, and `dist/buildos.js` of the project copy for the wrapper and the printed command. This shows the entry scripts of the Node.js processes that the probe observed in each step, by real path, and no more: a process that is not Node.js, or a Node.js process started with a cleared environment, is not observed, so it is neither named nor excluded (a limit in `tarball_mode.does_not_prove`). `buildos version --json` was not used: it reports the version and the source revision, not where the program ran from.

## Review Round 3 and the Final Fix Pass (Pull Request 12) (2026-11-27)

An independent review of pull request 12 gave FAIL on `873b319`: the clean tarball passed on three systems, but the report claimed more than the checks proved, and some guards were loose. Under the project stop rule (three review rounds, then one fix pass), this is the fix pass. No further review round follows. Where a guarantee could not be made true, the claim in the report and the docs is narrowed instead. Each fix is in a new commit on `feat/smoke-a-tarball` ([history record](../../../.make-docs/archive/history/2026-11-27-w1-r7-p9-smoke-a-release-tarball-final-fix-pass.md)). The step counts are unchanged (20 on Linux and macOS and 19 on Windows for `0.2.0`; 18 and 17 for a `0.1.0` tarball).

| Finding | Disposition and fix | Proof |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (blocker) the report claimed to prove which executable each step ran, while the probe sees only Node.js processes that keep `NODE_OPTIONS`; npm programs were allowed by a path suffix of any npm installation; on POSIX `a\b` and `a/b` compared equal | Fixed, and the claim narrowed. The preflight selects one npm installation, the npm next to the Node.js that runs the smoke, by real path, and the launch check allows only its exact program files (`bin/npm-cli.js`, `bin/npx-cli.js`, and on Windows `bin/npm-prefix.js`; `npmPrograms` in `scripts/smoke-source.ts`) and, in the wrapper step, the exact real path of the project's own `.os/scripts/pinned-version.cjs`. The preflight also requires that the probe observed its own npm process, exactly `bin/npm-cli.js`. `pathKey` treats `\` and `/` as one separator and names as case-insensitive only on Windows. The claims, the limits, the report field `launchers` (now `npm_programs`, `observed`, and `observes`), the check labels, `SECURITY.md` "Smoke Workflow", the runbook (steps c and h2), the round 2 section of this report, the P9 phase file status, and the pull request body say only what the probe shows (below). | `test/smoke-tarball.test.ts`: another npm installation's `npx-cli.js`, another project's `pinned-version.cjs`, a file outside the copy, and an unreadable record fail; `npm-prefix.js` counts only on Windows and only in the selected installation; on POSIX `/a\b` and `/a/b` differ, on Windows `C:\A\B\` equals `c:/a/b`; a Node.js process with a cleared environment leaves no record; every claim that rests on the probe holds the observation limit. |
| 2 (high) both Windows shim parsers accepted a target that was only in a comment | Fixed. No target is parsed. In the preflight on Windows, the selected npm's own `cmd-shim` (`<npm>/node_modules/cmd-shim`, which npm's `bin-links` uses) writes the canonical shims of each bin into a scratch folder outside the temporary root, with the same relative layout as an install (`node_modules/.bin/<name>` for `node_modules/build-os/<bin file>`, which holds the tarball's bytes); each installed shim (`<name>`, `<name>.cmd`, `<name>.ps1`) must be byte-equal to it. Nothing is normalized: `cmd-shim` 8 makes its output only from the relative path from the shim's folder to the bin file and the bin file's first line, and both are the same as in an install. A shim that differs fails, and the report names it and its byte counts. | Tests on every system, with npm's own `cmd-shim`: the shims that it writes for the bin file pass; a `.cmd` that holds the target only in a comment fails; a comment added to a real `.ps1` fails; shims written for another target fail (all three); a missing shell shim fails. On Windows CI, the real-npm tests compare the real shims of both routes with the canonical ones. |
| 3 (high) a caller's npm `node-options` removed the probe from the processes that npm started (20 of 20 fell to 18 of 20) | Fixed. Every process gets `npm_config_node_options` equal to the probe's `NODE_OPTIONS` (a caller's value in any spelling is dropped, like the cache, prefix, and bin-links settings), and the preflight reads `npm config get offline registry bin-links node-options` and requires the probe's value. | Real npm, no network: with `node-options=--no-warnings` in a caller npmrc and in the caller's environment (two spellings), the preflight reads the probe, and the probe observed the bin; without the forced value, the npmrc wins, and the probe observes only `npx-cli.js` (the review's failure). The real smoke with that npmrc passed every check (below). |
| 4 (medium) the stray-folder search skipped any folder named `_logs` or `_cacache` (a copy under `project/_logs` was missed) and matched names case-sensitively on Windows; an extra empty folder in an install was not a problem | Fixed. The search skips only this run's `<cache>/_cacache` and `<cache>/_logs`, by exact path, and on Windows matches `node_modules` and `build-os` in any case during the search. The install comparison now fails on any folder that holds no tarball file, also an empty one: a normal install of this tarball makes none (npm pack writes no folder entry; the real installs of both routes hold only the tarball's folders), so failing is right. `tarball_mode.compares` says so. | Real npm: a `build-os` below `project/_logs` and one below `work/_cacache` fail; one in the run's own cache store is not searched; `NODE_MODULES/Build-OS` is found with the Windows rule and not with the POSIX rule; an extra empty folder and a nested one in the project install, and a `node_modules` folder in the npx install, fail and are named; a normal install has only `dist`. |
| 5 (medium) both downloaded reports held absolute npm paths under the runner's tool cache, and an unexpected cache key was printed as it was | Fixed. npm's paths are cleaned to `{NPM}` (the selected installation, before `{HOME}`). A cache key other than the tarball's own file key shows only its kind (`make-fetch-happen:request-cache:(the rest of the key is not shown)`, `pacote:tarball:file:(another file; its name is not shown)`). As the last step, every string of the report loses any absolute path that the cleaning left (a POSIX path, or a Windows drive path) to `{ABSOLUTE-PATH}`, and the report records the count in `absolute_paths_removed`. | The stubbed script on a `0.1.0` and a `0.2.0` fixture tarball, with a cache entry whose key names an absolute path of a runner folder: the JSON and Markdown reports match no POSIX absolute path and no Windows drive path (the placeholders exempt), `absolute_paths_removed` is `0` (the cleaning alone removed them), npm's programs show as `{NPM}/bin/...`, and the cache failures show only the kinds. The scrub itself on POSIX and Windows paths, and on placeholders, URLs, and a `sha512` value, which it keeps. The real reports of CI (below). |
| 6 (medium) a second hand-started run cancelled the first | Fixed. A pull-request run keeps its group by ref (`buildos-smoke-pr-<ref>`, cancel in progress); a hand-started run has the group `buildos-smoke-dispatch-<run id>` and does not cancel. The runbook (steps c, h2, and k) says that each run is started and read on its own, by its own run ID. | `test/release-workflow.test.ts`: the exact concurrency block, one block only, and no group keyed by the ref alone. |

### What the Report Now Claims About Executables (Pull Request 12)

The direct-steps claim of `tarball_mode.proves` says, in part: "in each of these runs, the entry scripts of the Node.js processes that the launch probe observed were only the selected npm's own programs and that package's bin file, with that bin file at least once (A process that is not Node.js, or a Node.js process started with a cleared environment (without the probe in NODE_OPTIONS), is not observed.)". The wrapper and step 10 claims say the same for their steps, with the project's `.os/scripts/pinned-version.cjs` in step 9. `tarball_mode.does_not_prove` adds: "Every executable that a step ran. The launch probe (a --require preload in NODE_OPTIONS and npm's node-options) shows only the entry scripts of the Node.js processes that it observed in each step. A process that is not Node.js, or a Node.js process started with a cleared environment (without the probe in NODE_OPTIONS), is not observed. Such a process leaves no record, so the report cannot name it or show that it did not run." No report field, check label, or doc sentence says that the smoke proves which executable ran.

### The Missed Order (Steps h1 to i)

The runbook puts step j (the npm stage approval) last, after the checks h1 to h5 and the recorded publication approval of step i. The owner approved the stage right after the stage job, so these did not come before step j:

- h1, the stage is the reviewed file: not done. No `npm stage list`, `npm stage view`, or `npm stage download` ran, and the stage no longer exists. The transparency-log part of h1 was done after publication, on the registry tarball ([below](#transparency-log-lookup-runbook-h1-done-after-publication)).
- h2, the second run (the smoke on the asset of the published release `v0.2.0`, `source=release-tag`): not run, before or after publication. The release asset is byte-equal to the dry-run tarball that the first run (step c) tested (`cmp`), and to the registry tarball (`npm pack`, SHA-256 equal), and the registry smoke ran after publication.
- h4, the size and performance record: not recorded before step j. The size was known from step c; the record is below ([Retrospective Publication Review (0.2.0)](#retrospective-publication-review-020)). `PERF-002` did not run, as the runbook planned.
- h5, the publication review for the owner: not written before step j. It is written now, retrospectively ([below](#retrospective-publication-review-020)).
- i, the recorded publication approval: none was given before step j.

Who did what: the orchestrator had given the owner the steps after g; the owner missed them and approved the stage with 2FA. The runbook already says that this gate is owner-enforced, not technical: "Nothing technical stops an early approval. After step g, a maintainer can approve the stage with 2FA at once, in the CLI or on npmjs.com, and npm does not look at h1 to h5 or at step i." So the same order as for `0.1.0` (the npm approval before the checks) was missed again, by a different cause: for `0.1.0` the orchestrator's step list put the approval first ([First Publication of 0.1.0](#first-publication-of-010-2026-11-26)); for `0.2.0` the runbook had the right order, and the owner missed the instructions. No owner decision or approval is recorded here that the owner did not give.

What did run before the approval: every gate of the dry run (46020963025), the prepare run (46043008348), and the release run (46043810434), including the real-list deny-list jobs and the stage job's checks; the inspection and the smoke on the dry-run tarball on three systems (step c, run 46021631698); h3 (rollback by pin on the tarball, macOS); the owner's acceptance of the tarball (step d); the independent review of pull request 13; and the orchestrator's settings check (step f).

### Transparency Log Lookup (Runbook h1, Done After Publication)

Runbook h1 binds the staged file to release run 46043810434 and the tag `v0.2.0` through the transparency log. It did not run before the approval. It ran after publication, on the registry tarball (`npm pack build-os@0.2.0`), whose SHA-256 equals the reviewed entry; it is the file that the stage job staged (the stage job checked that digest before staging). curl -sS https://rekor.sigstore.dev/api/v1/log/entries/108e9186e8c5677aa877f1f771bbb5e622e9fb8d4ce8a7292bc40e23d6dd428cf7f355511e9e354e

### Rollback From 0.2.0 to 0.1.0 Through npx (F-P8-09)

What F-P8-09 asks ([Follow-ups (Post-Publication Checks)](#follow-ups-post-publication-checks)): prove rollback by version pin through `npx` to an earlier published version, `0.2.0` back to `0.1.0`, on a copied project, on three systems. The runbook (step k) runs it after the registry smoke, and it closes t16 and A72 when it passes. The guide's steps are chapter 4, "From 0.1.0 to 0.2.0" and "Roll back from 0.2.0 to 0.1.0" (`guide/content/04-install-and-configure-your-instance.md`).

No route in the repository does it on three systems. `scripts/published-smoke.ts` and `.github/workflows/buildos-smoke.yml` run one version (registry or tarball) and change no pin, and no other workflow or script runs the guide's upgrade and rollback steps. So the proof was done by hand on this one macOS machine.

Verified on 2026-11-27: macOS 27.2 arm64, the official Node.js 24.22.3 (`node-v24.22.3-darwin-arm64.tar.gz`, SHA-256 checked against the nodejs.org `SHASUMS256.txt`, unpacked into a temporary folder) with its npm 11.19.1, `/bin/sh`, a new empty npm cache, a new empty home folder, `PATH` set to that Node.js and the system folders only, and no `buildos` on `PATH`. Every `build-os` came from the public registry through `npx`; no local or global install of `build-os` was made at any point. A project was set up in `{TMP}/orig` (`git init`, `npx -y build-os@0.1.0 init --skip-make-docs`, a commit) and copied with `cp -Rp` to `{TMP}/proj`; the copy is the test project. The guide's steps ran as written in the copy:

| Step | Exit | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
